data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: ‘China Shock 2.0’ is crushing the West
data.description:
Robot vacuum cleaners are typically less noisy than their older, hand-operated cousins. But the volume of the Chinese-made versions is not the only quiet thing. They are also stealthily taking over the world.

Dreame, a company founded in Suzhou less than a decade ago, is now said to be the world’s biggest seller of robot vacuums. Its founder, 39-year-old Yu Hao, claims to be building a $100tn (£75tn) ecosystem of smart appliances and frontier tech.

After just two years in Britain, Dreame is still a relatively small player here. Euromonitor International put the company’s UK market share at 4pc last year.

But four Chinese companies control almost half the UK market. And their cheapest products are all priced below those of SharkNinja and Dyson, which manufacture in Asia but do at least some of the brain-work in the US and Britain, respectively.

When it comes to Chinese imports, most people think first of electric vehicles (EVs), which are swarming into markets worldwide, such as Jaecoo, a brand that has become the go-to for British consumers. It is certainly the prime battlefront, with Britain under growing pressure to mimic the EU’s tariffs of up to 45pc on EVs.

Beneath these headlines, however, cut-price Chinese imports of just about any manufactured product are now sweeping into the West and challenging local businesses.

Consumers love the low prices. But companies and governments across Europe now fear that the Chinese juggernaut will hoover up Western industries and jobs, and leave the Continent utterly dependent on the whims and will of Beijing.

The timing of this “China Shock 2.0” – the first shock was the flood of low-priced toys, clothes and other manufactured goods that hit in the early 2000s – is not a coincidence. In the past few years, Beijing has unmuzzled its most potent weapon to win the export war.

Chinese factories have long enjoyed advantages such as cheap workers and raw materials, generous subsidies and massive economies of scale. But now a new wave of cheap credit – that is, loans made on concessional or non-commercial terms – has swept through the Chinese manufacturing sector, unlocking the export tsunami.

“This is probably the single biggest component of China’s industrial policy,” says Camille Boullenois, a China expert at the Rhodium Group consultancy.

“It has been the most powerful and the most influential factor shaping the economic system in China, because the entire economic system is based on credit.”

‘Everything in China is political’

Ever since China’s banks pulled back from lending to households after the spectacular property crash of 2021, they have been scrambling to find enough borrowers.

And with the Chinese government ever more focused on ramping up high-tech and advanced manufacturing, that’s where the banks have been pouring all that surplus cash.

“There’s a natural herding in the way the Chinese private sector operates. Once everybody realised that manufacturing is where the political light was shining, then capital and human talent moved into manufacturing,” says David Lubin, of the think tank Chatham House.

The banks have become the pivotal enabler of Beijing’s ambition to ensure companies, such as Dreame, dominate global markets and supply chains.

“Lending is political, because everything in China is political. And credit is a political tool,” says Leo Austin, a businessman who advises multinationals on working in China.

These dirt-cheap loans mean that, unlike their Western rivals, many Chinese companies can receive capital on tap.

“There is always cash flow available to you, and you have no short-term fear around the viability of the business, so you can afford to be incredibly aggressive,” Austin says.

This has wrought a transformation in China that is little appreciated outside its borders.

Once there were private firms and state-owned enterprises. But now most companies are a hybrid: they have a private-sector management culture, but are almost entirely funded by government-sourced equity and state-backed lending.

Austin calls this model “state-capitalised private enterprises”. The emerging Chinese high-tech giants are almost all cut from this cloth.

Chinese banks are bound by law to lend money “in accordance with the needs of the national economic and social development, and under the guidance of the industrial policies of the state”.

And they do. Beijing’s corporate debt totals about 138pc of GDP, almost double the ratio in the US. But Chinese companies’ interest costs amount to less than 1pc of turnover, compared with 5pc for their American peers.

The effect of this fresh wave of cheap credit has been immediate.

China’s domination

Between 2021 and 2024, the number of products where China accounts for more than half of global exports nearly doubled, from 192 to 315.

China’s trade surplus will again surpass $1tn this year. The surplus with both Germany and France has doubled in the past year. For the EU as a whole, it amounts to more than €1bn (£840m) a day.

Although this export surge makes China appear like a rising economic superpower, the boom in cheap credit and factory exports has a dark side.

Companies are exporting their credit-fuelled output because Chinese households, burnt by the property crash, are not spending. At home, Chinese companies are forced into painful discounting wars just to move stock.

Profitability has plummeted and one in three companies is loss-making. Without the exports, which often provide more than 40pc of revenue, many businesses would be unviable.

Yet the banks keep lending and lending. Often, they have to discount the interest rate simply because otherwise the borrower would go bust.

Instead, it is European competitors who are absorbing the blow. In Britain, some have complained to the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA), which can impose quotas or tariffs.

The TRA has sought to protect local manufacturers from cut-price Chinese imports of everything from ceramics to ironing boards, tyres and cherry-pickers.

One recent TRA ruling noted that Chinese companies “have access to preferential financing, and access to financing from institutions which implement public policy objectives or otherwise do not act independently of the state”.

The TRA added: “They have more flexibility and can adjust their business and pricing strategies to maximise their export sales and gain market share in the UK, even if they would have otherwise made negative profit margins.”

No easy answers

Given that the Government is aware of the problem, many businesses want to see it push back harder. “There are probably plenty of stones that could be unturned,” one industry veteran says.

Rhodium’s Boullenois says the same is true in Europe, where Brussels’s trade directorate is overwhelmed with business requests for protection.

“We’re protecting too few products. Our defences need to be much broader, and work much faster,” she says.

But if the EU and US protect their own markets, more of the ultra-cheap Chinese exports will simply shift to Asia, Africa and Latin America – displacing European and American rivals in those countries’ markets.

“We normally look at how much is China selling to the EU. A lot less time is spent thinking about how many EU products the Chinese manufacturers are displacing in foreign markets – and it’s huge,” says Joe Peissel, of the consultancy Trivium China.

The battle against China’s factories is on in earnest. But as long as the Chinese are backed up by the bazooka of the country’s banking system, it will be a war that the West will struggle to win.

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: Europe’s gas shortage could open the door for Putin
data.description:
Donald Trump says he has settled eight wars, but the biggest prize – peace between Russia and Ukraine – still eludes and frustrates him. The president now insists, however, that a “big, beautiful agreement” is on the cards.

His negotiators, Steve Witkoff, the property developer, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law, will head to Abu Dhabi this week for the first face-to-face peace talks with Russia and Ukraine since February.

This three-way negotiation has squeezed out the other key players with skin in the game: the Europeans. Trump himself said last week that the deal “might involve all of Europe”.

However, Kushner is not worried. “We will consult closely with our European partners on the sidelines,” he said on X last Friday.

Although the Europeans are sidelined, their priority is clear: a peace deal must neutralise the threat of Russian aggression.

But the Americans have muddied the waters. Reports suggest they are pushing for a peace deal that would controversially include the resumption of Russian gas exports to Europe.

The Europeans have spent the past four years painfully weaning themselves off an addiction to Vladimir Putin’s energy bounty. They are now in the final furlong of a legally binding process to shut out Russian gas permanently.

Grounds to reopen Russian pipelines

The plan is to end shipments of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) by New Year’s Day and phase out the last pipeline imports by this time next year.

But if the Americans have their way, they might open the door for Putin to start rebuilding his once-mighty energy leverage over Europe.

Most analysts say there’s little chance that Brussels or Kyiv would countenance any return to relying on the Russians to keep the lights on.

“While there are EU members in the east, like Slovakia, that have always sought to maintain Russian gas flows, the view from Berlin and Paris et al is that the ban on Russian gas from Jan 1 will go ahead,” says Bill Farren-Price, of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

But European households and industries are struggling with soaring energy costs, and countries such as Germany and the Netherlands have not managed to store enough gas this year to be sure of seeing out the winter.

The International Energy Agency warned last week that if Trump doesn’t settle the Iran war soon, and if the winter is long and cold, Europe could be paying elevated prices for gas all the way into next summer.

For every European politician or industrialist who baulks at the Americans’ freewheeling dealmaking with the Kremlin, there might be another who is sorely tempted by the prospect of cheaper gas.

“Although pretty much all the countries around the Baltic Sea would be staunchly against it, Germany would be an interesting case. Germany politically is mostly against it, but German industrialists would probably be quite for it,” said Sergey Vakulenko, of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre.

The deal might spur Slovakia and Hungary, which still rely on Russian gas piped through Turkey and the Balkans, to push for a relaxation of the EU-wide ban.

And if Marine Le Pen wins the French presidency next April, she may join their cause. In Germany, the ascendant Alternative für Deutschland party has called for the Russian pipelines to reopen.

A Russian energy renaissance in Europe may still seem far-fetched to many. But as the Americans plan what Kushner calls “an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability”, Putin can dare to dream.

The trickle of reports on the American gas blueprint suggests Kushner and Witkoff have been beavering away at it for several months.

Reuters reported in early October that the pair had proposed marshalling American investors to reopen the Nord Stream pipeline, which used to carry vast amounts of Russian gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea.

Berlin mothballed the pipelines after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and later that year they were sabotaged in a series of underwater explosions.

Kushner reportedly floated the plan with Kirill Dmitriev, one of Putin’s closest associates. Dmitriev has publicly advocated resuming gas sales to Germany. He has held talks with US energy officials and was in the White House last week to meet Trump himself.

The midterm elections handed control of Congress to the Democrats, who have little appetite to lift US sanctions on Nord Stream. The victors take the reins on Capitol Hill from January, so Trump needs either to strike a deal by Christmas or move to Plan B.

Europe is running out of options

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Kushner and Witkoff had also proposed selling Russian gas to Europe via a US intermediary to skirt the EU’s ban.

This plan would allow Kyiv to earn transit fees from its pipeline network. And the sales revenue would be held in an escrow account to ensure that Putin could not spend the funds on fighting Ukraine.

Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said last week that such a deal was not possible now, given “the situation on the ground”. But he did not rule it out.

Vakulenko, of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, doubts this particular plan will fly. “When they start to discuss escrow accounts, that’s a big no-no for Russia. And I also don’t think Trump’s leverage over the Europeans is that strong at the moment,” he says.

Yet surging gas prices are exerting real leverage on Europe, which has almost tripled since the Iran war began in late February.

The EU’s storage tanks are only 74pc full, at least 10 percentage points below the norm for this time of year. Germany’s are only at 60pc capacity.

The Europeans are competing with Asia for expensive cargoes from the US, and banking on the constancy of Norway’s output. This has made the task of weaning the Continent off Russian gas much harder.

Data by think tank Bruegel suggest the EU has been importing about 380 million cubic metres of Russian gas per week recently – exactly the same amount as at this time last year.

The EU still relies on Russia for between 12pc and 15pc of its gas. In August, the bloc bought €756m (£630m) of Russian pipeline gas and €323m of LNG, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

It looks like a tall order, or at least a costly one, to shut out Russian LNG by Jan 1.

The law gives Brussels the power to pause the ban temporarily if energy supplies are under serious threat, but cost alone is not expected to be sufficient grounds.

“Even before the Middle East conflict, there were some people in the market who thought the EU might relax that deadline, push it back until the spring, given the storage situation. We don’t think that will be the case,” says Tom Marzec-Manser, at energy analysis firm Wood Mackenzie.

He adds that even if the Europeans needed Russian gas, they would be conscious of the risk of handing leverage and influence to Putin.

“The moment you do it, you’re put in a position of weakness. You’ve cornered yourself somewhat, from a foreign-policy perspective.”

Dan Jorgensen, the EU’s energy commissioner, is of the same mind. “I certainly would not trust Russia, even if there were peace tomorrow,” he said last month.

But if Trump did, against the odds, deliver peace tomorrow, Russian gas could be back on the table. The Europeans may not trust Putin. The question is whether, faced with the temptation of cheap energy, they can even trust themselves.

data.title: How Virgin Media O2’s failed takeover gambit cost 4,000 jobs
data.description:
When Mike Fries, the 63-year-old boss of Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) parent company Liberty Global, mounted a defence of the £2bn broadband takeover he had engineered, his strategy was scattergun.

“Who is going to build a scale-based competitor to BT Openreach?” he said at a conference in London this year. “Who has the capital, the wherewithal, the customers? I don’t think there’s anybody else.”

Criticism levelled at the deal by rivals was merely “sour grapes”, he insisted, while simultaneously threatening to pull investment in the UK if it was blocked on competition grounds.

But his warnings fell on deaf ears. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) signalled last month that it was likely to block VMO2’s takeover of Netomnia on fears it would push up prices for customers.

The apparent failure has set off fears that VMO2, owner of Britain’s second-largest broadband network after BT, is headed for danger over its £22bn debt pile.

The Netomnia takeover promised a vital lifeline to help pay down this debt. With that deal on the ropes, bosses are now preparing to cut 4,000 jobs in an attempt to strip out £800m of costs.

It is a sobering shake-up for a company hoping to secure its position as the second-largest player in Britain’s cut-throat broadband market. Yet some analysts warn that it might not be enough.

VMO2, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, was formed through a £31bn merger of Virgin Media and O2 in 2021.

The deal gave it the scale to compete against BT as a converged mobile and broadband operator. But it also loaded the combined company up with debt.

While Telefonica’s O2 arrived debt-free, Liberty’s Virgin Media contributed a £11.3bn debt pile, a legacy of the chaotic cable rollout of the 1990s.

A major debt recapitalisation, which was used to fund a £7.1bn payout to the parent companies, pushed this up above £18bn. Total debt has since climbed further to around £22.4bn.

In many ways, it was a textbook deal for Liberty Global, the Bermuda-domiciled telecoms group controlled by cable cowboy John Malone. The company had partly been attracted to Virgin Media by the lawful tax avoidance opportunities offered by its historical debts.

Liberty Global, which has its London base in plush offices just off the King’s Road in Chelsea, has gained a reputation for debt-fuelled takeovers and financial engineering. Its other UK investments include Formula E, ITV and film producer Lionsgate.

To date, the merger has paid off handsomely. Liberty and Telefónica have extracted more than £12bn from VMO2 through cash payouts and dividends.

Fries, meanwhile, has been paid more than $200m ($149m) since the formation of VMO2. Over the past decade, his pay stands at $484m, including $123m pocketed in 2019 alone.

Bosses argue that VMO2 has invested £11bn in the UK since the merger. Yet while its shareholders were feathering their nests, the backdrop for VMO2 was beginning to darken.

Fierce competition from a flood of “alt-net” rivals and lower-than-expected uptake of full-fibre have put pressure on all broadband providers. Meanwhile, rising interest costs have pushed up the cost of servicing debts.

Fitch Ratings downgraded VMO2 to B+ in June, pushing it deeper into speculative “junk” territory.

Among the reasons cited for the downgrade were a ballooning debt pile, shrinking revenues and cash flow, growing competition and the large funding requirements of its fibre build.

But the downgrade risks exacerbating VMO2’s troubles, making it harder to borrow new money to pay down existing debt. Where it can obtain new debt, the company is likely to find borrowing has become more expensive.

The warning that spooked the markets the most was that VMO2’s debt-to-Ebitda (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) ratio of 6.1 times had severely breached safe thresholds. It has since reduced to 5.56 times.

With concerns mounting, a sell-off began over the summer. The company’s US junk bonds were selling for as little as 42p in the pound, suggesting traders believe there is a slim chance of them being fully repaid. Rivals and VMO2 insiders believe the company faces inevitable financial restructuring.

It wasn’t meant to be this way for Fries and his charges. For VMO2, the Netomnia deal offered a lifeline. The complex transaction would see Nexfibre – a joint venture between Liberty Global, Telefónica and French infrastructure fund InfraVia – take control of Britain’s second-largest alt-net.

Under the terms of the deal, VMO2 would be handed a 15pc stake in Nexfibre in exchange for migrating 4.6 million homes onto its network. Crucially, it would incur no net-cash cost. Instead, VMO2 would receive £950m, which would help pay down debt, though it would also be liable for future fees to access Nexfibre’s network.

It was a deal that aimed to reward all parties. What bosses had failed to consider, however, was the CMA’s dogged response.

Fries this week described the regulator’s intervention as a “bit of a wake-up call”, adding: “Never did we anticipate that this transaction with Netomnia would encounter such fierce resistance.”

The competition watchdog has not yet reached a verdict on the deal, but VMO2 has already smashed the glass on a punishing cost-cutting plan.

Around 4,000 jobs are expected to go, delivering £300m in savings. The company will halt upgrades to its broadband network, while it is considering scrapping its dividend.

The cost-cutting programme was brought forward in an effort to ease concerns in the bond market. Some observers note that the heavy cuts may also help to strengthen VMO2’s case to the CMA, which will issue its final decision by Dec 15.

The programme has underwhelmed many analysts, however, who argue they were already overdue.

Matthew Howett, at Assembly Research, says that VMO2 “needed to get their house in order anyway”. He adds: “There was an element of this that needed to happen anyway, and we’re now just seeing it in the cold light of day and it’s made a bit more critical by that [CMA] decision.”

James Ratzer, at New Street Research, says: “If you look at what’s going on within their business, they have been paying out dividends to the shareholders while revenues have been under pressure and the debt burden has been growing. So I think cost-cutting is a necessity.”

Perhaps more concerningly for VMO2 and its future finances, however, are the challenges in its underlying business. In the age of full-fibre BT, its broadband business depends on consumers paying more for an arguably inferior technology.

The company shed a further 23,000 customers in the third quarter, while its average revenue per broadband customer fell 5pc to £45.83. Analysts point both to tough competition and a reduction in the number of additional services, such as TV, that customers are taking.

Ratzer describes falling service revenues as the “melting ice cube” in VMO2’s business.

There is something else at play, too. VMO2, which has long faced criticism for its poor customer service, has been hit by Ofcom’s “one-touch switching” policy, which came into force in September 2024.

“One-touch switching has definitely been a very damaging thing for their business, and that’s what’s caused them to change strategy,” says Ratzer. “Now it’s become easier for customers to leave, they’ve suddenly had to change tack to be more proactive with price reductions.”

VMO2 argues that an operational turnaround is underway under Lyssa McGowan, a former Pets at Home and Sky executive who was brought in to lead the company’s consumer operations this summer.

McGowan served at Sky under Stephen van Rooyen, the media giant’s former UK boss who was appointed to lead Ziggo Group, another Liberty-owned telecoms operator that is being lined up for a stock market float next year. She in turn has appointed two other former Sky executives to lead the Virgin Media and O2 brands.

But the appointments have fuelled speculation that Liberty is preparing to parachute the well-regarded van Rooyen to replace long-serving Lutz Schüler as chief executive of VMO2, though sources close to the company denied this.

A VMO2 spokesman said: “Virgin Media O2 continues to be a vastly successful telecoms combination and a major competitive force in the market with strong underlying assets. The decisions and actions we’re taking now are necessary to transform for the future.”

The spokesman pointed to VMO2’s £11bn investment, its 5G and satellite mobile offering and its gigabit broadband network reaching almost 19 million homes, adding: “There’s work to do and challenges to navigate but Virgin Media O2 is focused on delivering for the long-term.”

A Telefónica spokesperson said: “Telefónica has invested more than €33.3bn (£277bn) in the UK. In 2005, we made the strategic decision to enter the UK market through the acquisition of O2 and, in 2020, we announced the merger of O2 and Virgin Media. These decisions reflect our commitment to the country for more than 20 years.

“VMO2 remains the strongest challenger to BT/Openreach in a highly competitive sector where other relevant players are under financial challenges. We believe VMO2 is the result of a successful integration, with a strong competitive position and a valuable asset base. It is now undertaking the transformation needed to position the business for the future.”

Still, with the business under pressure, VMO2 is facing searching questions over its future.

There is a real concern in the market that the company may default on its debts, with focus centred on £1.6bn of debt maturing at the start of 2029. A further £12.3bn of maturities then fall between 2030 and 2032.

Enders Analysis estimates that refinancing this debt at current prices would cost VMO2 at least an extra £1bn in interest costs, an amount it describes as “ruinous”.

In fact, the prices of some bonds have plunged to levels that suggest investors believe there is little-to-no chance of repayment.

“The market’s telling you a restructuring is an inevitability when bond prices are at that level,” says Ratzer.

Sona Asset Management, the London-based hedge fund that specialises in distressed debt and restructuring, has stepped up its exposure to VMO2’s high-yield bonds in recent months.

Sona, along with fellow creditors BlackRock and Pimco, recently tapped the law firm Millbank to advise on the fallout from the faltering Netomnia deal.

Vulture funds are also understood to have begun snapping up the company’s junior debt after the recent sell-off. They are seen as positioning to drive a hard bargain in the expected restructuring discussions, potentially including swapping some of the debt for shares in VMO2, which may ultimately make its way to the public markets.

An alternative would be for shareholders to inject more equity into the company in exchange for a debt write-down.

The Enders analysts added: “VMO2 simply has to regain the confidence of the debt markets, or it will be forced into debt restructuring, with its current shareholders having their shareholding significantly diluted and/or having to inject further funds.”

With pressure rising, Fries this week insisted that Liberty Global did not intend to put corporate cash into its telecoms business.

Pressed on whether he could be forced to put cash into VMO2 as part of a restructuring, however, he demurred: “This is not a crisis, so I’m not prepared to address that hypothetical at all.”

data.title: Labour peer lined up as new Thames Water chairman
data.description:
Thames Water’s lenders have lined up a Labour peer to chair the company as Andy Burnham pushes to take public control of the embattled utility.

Lord Hutton, a former Cabinet minister, will become the most senior figure at Thames if a consortium of creditors succeeds in its £10bn rescue bid for the group.

London & Valley Water said Lord Hutton would be installed as chairman if its ownership bid succeeds, supported by telecoms veteran Mike McTighe who was named vice-chairman.

Hiring Lord Hutton may placate some Labour figures opposed to the creditors’ ownership of Thames.

The 71-year old held several senior roles between 1997 and 2010, serving as work and pensions secretary in Sir Tony Blair’s government and business secretary and then defence secretary under Gordon Brown.

However, as a staunch Blairite, Lord Hutton admitted to privately briefing that Mr Brown would be “a f------ disaster” if he became prime minister. The comments were made in 2006 when Sir Tony was facing an internal coup from Mr Brown and his supporters.

London & Valley Water’s move comes as the group of lenders attempts to head off Mr Burnham’s calls to bring water companies into public ownership.

The creditors are finalising a revised £10bn rescue deal it hopes will win over Ofwat, the regulator. The proposal is expected to be tabled in the next few weeks.

However, the environment, food and rural affairs select committee urged the Government to reject the plan last week.

The news of Lord Hutton’s appointment comes as the Prime Minister looks for alternative ways to bring Thames under public control.

Mr Burnham has reportedly ordered government officials to come up with more radical solutions for how to address the debacle at Britain’s largest water company, according to The Guardian.

He has previously expressed support for nationalising Thames Water. However, it is thought the Prime Minister has been warned that the Government cannot afford to do so.

Mr Burnham has been unable to find a way to bring the company under public control without spending billions in taxpayer money or risk getting caught up in a drawn out legal battle.

Officials believe that changes to the “special administration regime” would make it less challenging for the Government to take firms such as Thames Water into state control in the coming years.

Another idea is for the Government to forgo £100m of fines owed by Thames in return for a stake in the group.

Lord Hutton said: “People living in London and the Thames Valley have the right to expect the highest possible standards of customer service and proper environmental stewardship from their water company, and that will be our focus as we look to the future.”

London & Valley Water was created by a group of fund managers, including Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital. They have already lent the stricken company £3bn to keep it afloat.

The lenders collectively hold £17bn of Thames Water’s £21bn debt pile.

data.title: Troubled housebuilder to shut offices and slash jobs in turnaround scramble
data.description:
Vistry is to shut down half its offices across the country and slash jobs as it grapples with a nationwide property downturn.

The embattled housebuilder said it would close 13 of its 25 offices in a move Adam Daniels, its chief executive, said was “difficult but necessary” as it seeks to save £50m next year.

The company expects its average daily debt pile to swell to £800m in the second half of the year, up from £771m during the same period last year.

It is unclear how many of Vistry’s 4,500 staff are at risk under the changes, which will come into effect in January.

Vistry revealed a record loss of £661m for the first half of the financial year in September, and said it planned to build fewer homes as rising mortgage rates triggered by the Iran war’s impact on inflation dampened demand.

Estate agency Savills expects house prices to fall until at least the second half of 2028, with London, the South East and the East of England worst affected.

The average five-year fixed mortgage rate is currently 5.99pc, according to Moneyfacts - up from 4.96pc at the start of February before Donald Trump ordered the first strikes on Iran.

Vistry blamed its struggles on “difficult” market conditions, nervous home buyers and affordability constraints.

Mr Daniels said the firm had taken “decisive action to create a smaller, more focused and disciplined business”.

Vistry’s share price slumped by more than 4pc to £2.77 on Thursday. Its shares have tumbled by almost 57pc since the start of the year.

Its struggles come despite securing £350m from the Government in August to build affordable and social homes.

Labour had vowed to oversee 1.5m houses being built during this parliament. However, many developers and experts have warned the weak market means the target is effectively dead in the water.

Official figures show that only 306,640 housing starts have taken place across the UK since Labour took power in July 2024. It means Andy Burnham must oversee the construction of nearly 1.2 million more homes by August 2029 at the latest to hit Labour’s target.

The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates today for the first time in three years from 3.75pc to 4pc, adding to the strain on mortgage borrowers.

data.title: Lime bike jousters defy warnings from company to stop
data.description:
“Joust, joust, joust,” the crowds jeered, as two knights charged towards one another, lances raised.

You might be forgiven for thinking the scene had been lifted from medieval Camelot.

But, atop a neon-green steed, the “knights” in question were taking part in a new phenomenon called “Lime bike jousting”, which sees riders on the rental e-bikes charge at one another brandishing striped poles.

Jack Carden, an artist, and actor Camtholomew the First, whose real name is Cameron Carnegie-Brown, staged their first duel earlier this month, drawing hundreds of spectators to London Fields, east London.

Footage of the first duel showed the pair charging towards one another on the e-bikes, dressed in chainmail, red and black cloaks and full suits of armour.

Each wielded a striped lance as they attempted to knock their opponent from his saddle.

But their medieval enthusiasm was not shared by Lime.

The company said in a statement: “While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first. Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting.”

The company also discouraged riders from “attempting similar events”.

The men defied the warnings to stop and took part in another event on Saturday, called Lime bike Jousting 2: No Horses, No Mercy.

More than 5,000 people had registered their interest within a day of the invitation going online.

The organisers received police approval for the mass gathering and dropped the exact location coordinates just an hour and a half before the duel.

Hundreds of spectators descended on the park in an assortment of medieval finery and Hallowe’en fancy dress, transforming the east London park into a makeshift jousting arena.

Mr Carden said before the contest began: “This is a very special moment, not just for us, but for London... this is the most viewed joust of the modern era.”

The combatants were helped into their armour by their entourage before mounting their electric steeds, decorated for the occasion. “Ring maidens” in medieval dress set out the various rounds.

The pair battled through five rounds, with Mr Carnegie-Brown eventually claiming victory after landing the decisive blow.

Both Mr Carden and Mr Carnegie-Brown said that crowd safety was their “biggest priority” at the event. There were organising stewards to help with crowd control and health professionals on hand.

Hackney council said it did not give permission for the event to be held in the borough, but organisers claimed that they had informed the council that the event was going ahead with a full safety team.

The two “knights” competed in the duel for charity, raising more than £1,200.

The charities include The Bike Project, which fixes second-hand bikes and gives them to refugees, Honour Thy Woman Group, a domestic abuse charity, and the Mental Health Foundation.

There was even a seal of approval from the world of traditional jousting.

Andy Deane, the captain of the Royal Armouries jousting team in Leeds, said it was a “joy” to see the bike jousting “capturing the spectacle” of the medieval sport.

“This is absolutely a legitimate form of jousting,” he said following the first joust.

Mr Carden told The Telegraph: “We informed the council it was going ahead. We had a full safety team with first aiders, safety stewards, clean up crew, and had a chat with police before going ahead to ensure everything would be safe.

“We have been in touch with Lime from the first joust and they have at no point told us not to go ahead, merely to reinforce safety messages.”

Lime has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Buses to be driven by teenagers as operators face staff shortages
data.description:
Teenagers will be allowed to drive buses for school trips and weddings as part of a government shake-up to tackle shortages.

Ministers confirmed on Friday they were exploring changes to licensing rules that currently stop 18 and 19-year-olds from undertaking certain kinds of journeys.

Currently, they can qualify as bus and coach drivers, but operators can only assign them regular routes of less than 50 kilometres (31 miles).

The Department for Transport (DfT) wants to give teenagers the right to take on longer journeys and “non-regular” jobs as well, such as school trips, weddings, transport for football matches and holiday tours.

As well as tackling driver shortages, the DfT said the shake-up would provide more opportunities for young people at a time when around one million aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training – also known as Neets.

However, the Government said it was also considering potential safety issues with young drivers more prone to being in accidents than their elders.

It acknowledged that only limited data were available on young bus drivers, but pointed to wider road transport data showing that nearly a quarter of collisions resulting in deaths last year involved drivers aged 17 to 24.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for buses and local transport, said: “We want to clear the roadblocks that have been preventing too many young people from getting behind the wheel of a rewarding career.

“The proposed changes will help more 18 and 19-year-olds get into the bus and coach sector, giving them the opportunity to build skills, earn a living and develop a rewarding career, while maintaining the highest standards of road safety.”

This came after ministers separately lowered the minimum age for train drivers in Britain from 20 to 18 earlier this year amid a youth worklessness crisis.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has described the current number of jobless young people as an “economic catastrophe and moral failure”.

In consultation documents published on Friday, the DfT said there were an estimated 113,900 bus and coach drivers in the UK but only around 500 were aged 18 or 19.

Keith McNally, of the Confederation of Passenger Transport, which represents bus and coach operators, said the sector had also been battling a recruitment crisis since the Covid pandemic, which prompted some older drivers to retire while problems securing tests stopped new ones from qualifying.

“We’ve had shortages, so we think the opportunity to bring in more young people and let them experience what our industry has to offer is very positive,” he said.

The current rules “have some inconsistencies”, Mr McNally added, with teenage lorry-drivers not facing equivalent curbs.

At the moment, 18 and 19-year-olds can qualify as bus and coach drivers, but they are restricted to driving regular scheduled services of less than 31 miles.

This effectively means they can take on most local bus routes, school bus work and some inter-city services run by the likes of National Express and Flixbus.

However, it excludes them from school field-trips, football-team transport, weddings and other private-hire contracts.

Such non-regular services make up the majority of trips carried out by the coach sector, Mr McNally said.

He also sought to ease safety concerns by claiming that young drivers of buses and heavy goods vehicles are “just as safe as people who are older than them”.

“We don’t believe there are legitimate safety issues here, not least because of the training and selection processes that companies have got in place,” he said.

The Government’s consultation closes on Dec 18.

data.title: 114-year-old Wiltshire tea room closes after ‘relentless tax rises’
data.description:
A historic tea room in one of England’s most affluent market towns has blamed “relentless tax rises” for its decision to close permanently after 114 years.

The Polly Tea Rooms has been a fixture of Marlborough’s grand high street in Wiltshire since 1912, when pioneering suffragette Janet McCloud and her business partner, Jean Leith Hay, set it up.

However, a notice went up in the window this week declaring “sorry we are closed”.

It said the venue was shutting its doors for good because of “relentless tax rises and overhead costs, plus another minimum wage increase”.

The notice said these burdens came at a time “when there is an ongoing cost of living crisis affecting our customers’ ability to eat out”, adding that “it is simply impossible to run a high street business in the UK in these circumstances”.

The Polly Tearooms, renowned in its early days as a safe place for local women to meet because of its suffragette connection, has served breakfasts, lunches and teas to residents and tourists for more than a century.

At the time of closure, a cream tea for two cost £23, while the all-day full English breakfast was priced at £12.95.

David Clarke, the then owner, put it up for sale last year and listed it at £460,000, according to the Wiltshire Gazette and Herald. The listing has since been removed from the website of the agents handling the sale, Every Masson & Furby.

It is the latest business to shut on a high street voted the best in Britain as recently as 2024.

Retailers across the UK have complained about the impact of Labour’s tax-raising Budgets.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, increased employer National Insurance contributions, while a higher minimum wage and steeper business rates also made life harder for bars and restaurants.

However, the town, to which King John of England granted a charter in 1204 and which is home to Marlborough College, has faced a series of high-street closures in recent years.

Rick Stein, a celebrity chef, shut his fish restaurant last October after nearly a decade of trading.

Dan Bond, who runs restaurant Dan’s at The Crown, told the BBC last year: “Over a year ago we had 14 independent restaurants; we had five pubs doing food along the high street. Now I think we’ve got nine – only nine of those restaurants going, and only two of those pubs doing food.

“For us as small business owners, it feels like we’re working really hard just to pay the Government.”

The former WH Smith branch was also converted into a TG Jones outlet, which closed last month.

Other losses include the Rejuvenesce Beauty Salon in Hughenden Yard in Marlborough, which shut its doors in January, and fashion brand Mint Velvet, which permanently closed its Marlborough shop in May.

data.title: Poundland wins last-minute reprieve in rescue talks
data.description:
Poundland has secured a last-minute lifeline after its US owner said it supported an extension of rescue talks.

The High Court has granted the retailer, which is owned by investment firm Gordon Brothers, 10 more days to find a buyer before administrators are appointed.

The decision on Thursday removes the immediate threat of collapse after an initial deadline to secure a new owner expired overnight.

In a closed-door hearing in front of MPs on Wednesday, Gordon Brothers bosses said they would support the extension to the deadline to allow discussions with potential bidders to continue.

Poundland’s management team submitted an application to the High Court to roll over an existing notice to appoint administrators at AlixPartners, which was filed on Oct 29.

A statement from the Poundland board said: “Our stores remain open as usual during this period, and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.”

Gordon Brothers, which acquired Poundland for just £1 last summer, agreed to unlock around £10m from the company’s balance sheet on Tuesday to support the business.

A spokesman for Gordon Brothers said it backed the board’s decision, adding: “This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment.

“With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.

“We are in discussions with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and we have also received several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business.”

The US firm had been accused of starving the company of funding in an effort to push it into insolvency and sell the business off for parts.

It rejected a bid for the entire Poundland business from Ireland-based Martin Property Group because of the bidder’s unwillingness to repay a £30m shareholder loan.

This prompted a backlash from politicians including Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, who said he was demanding answers from the retailer’s owners.

Political scrutiny has been intense because Poundland’s demise would represent the biggest high street collapse since BHS went bust in 2016 and put 12,000 jobs at risk.

A number of suppliers, who have been left unpaid, have also urged the Government to block an administration.

Mark Newton-Jones, the European head of Gordon Brothers, escaped public scrutiny at the closed-door hearing of the business select committee on Wednesday after he warned that a “show trial” could derail efforts to find a buyer.

Joshua Reynolds, the Liberal Democrat MP for Maidenhead who sits on the committee, said MPs remained concerned that Gordon Brothers had “jeopardised the business”.

Mr Reynolds said: “Gordon Brothers have extracted £18.3m in fees from a business that they say is on a knife-edge.

“Evidence that Gordon Brothers presented to the committee today was directly refuted by Poundland management less than an hour later.

“So we will be calling Gordon Brothers back to a hearing at a time when it will not jeopardise the sale process.”

It is understood that Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group about a potential rescue deal, while it has also received an offer from Xyra Group Holdings, a little-known London investment firm.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland last June with a promise to provide “the financing to support the substantial turnaround of this iconic retailer”, which has a network of more than 600 stores.

It then put the company up for sale in September, though it is thought the US firm may have favoured selling the business off piecemeal.

Turnaround firm Modella Capital, retailer B&M, Poundstretcher owner Fortress and The Range’s CDS Superstores have all expressed interest in buying at least some stores.

Speaking to Sky News after the hearing, Barry Williams, Poundland’s managing director, confirmed that the company’s directors would hold a board meeting tonight on the company’s future, adding he was “fighting” on behalf of staff.

A spokesman for the Poundland board said last month that it was in talks with “several established retail operators” to sell certain stores.

“Collectively, these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs.”

AlixPartners declined to comment.
