data.title: ITV takeover sparks fears of White House meddling in news
data.description:
Lisa Nandy has ordered regulators to carry out a review of Sky’s £1.6bn takeover of ITV, citing concerns that the broadcaster could fall victim to interference by Donald Trump.

The Culture Secretary has told Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to draw up reports on the merger, which would see US-owned Sky take control of ITV’s channels and streaming service.

Ofcom will be required to consider the effect of the deal on freedom of expression and plurality of views in news media, while the CMA will review the effect on Britain’s broadcasting market.

The swoop has triggered concerns about the British broadcaster falling into foreign ownership, as well as the effect on news provision in the UK.

In a letter to Sky, Ms Nandy said both US cable giant Comcast – which owns Sky – and its subsidiary NBCUniversal were facing “ongoing political and regulatory scrutiny” in the US.

This includes an investigation launched by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), a regulator led by Brendan Carr, an ally of Mr Trump, over its agreements with local stations in the US.

The FCC launched a separate investigation last year into Comcast’s diversity policies.

Ms Nandy wrote: “There is a question over whether, in the absence of undertakings, consequences of such scrutiny in the US could affect Sky or ITV’s ability to report freely.”

Mr Trump’s assault on the media has been a hallmark of his second term, with the US president filing a $10bn (£7.4bn) defamation lawsuit against the BBC over a misleading edit of a Panorama documentary.

A judge has ruled that that Mr Trump must face questions from lawyers before the end of the year.

But the US president has reserved particular animosity for Comcast, branding Brian Roberts, the chief executive, a “disgrace to the integrity of broadcasting”.

Despite this, the US company donated $7.5m to help fund Mr Trump’s new White House ballroom.

Mr Trump’s administration has also clashed with Ofcom, claiming that Britain’s new online safety laws were harming free speech.

Alongside the public interest intervention notice (PIIN), Ms Nandy will also expand existing laws, which currently only include broadcast TV to cover on-demand programming.

The Culture Secretary, who previously said she was “minded to intervene”, has given the regulators until Jan 27 to report back, after which she will decide whether to refer the deal to a more detailed investigation.

Dame Carolyn McCall, ITV’s chief executive, previously said she expected the deal to be subject to an in-depth review lasting up to 18 months.

Sky agreed a deal in July to take control of the broadcaster behind shows including I’m a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and Love Island.

The transaction does not include ITV’s lucrative production business, which will remain a standalone company on the London Stock Exchange.

Ms Nandy also raised concerns about the power of the combined company in its home market, which together with the BBC would hold an 86pc share of all linear news and current affairs viewing in the UK.

She warned that this duopoly could lead to an “insufficient plurality of views”, particularly if Sky and ITV were to merge their news operations.

Ms Nandy raised particular concerns about how this would affect regional news, warning that the broadcasters could face commercial incentives to cut costs by merging or closing regional newsrooms or sharing content between them.

Bosses have pledged to continue ITV’s supply deal with ITN until at least 2031, while Sky News’s independence is guaranteed until 2028 under a legally binding agreement with Comcast.

Ms Nandy said she was not aware of any evidence to suggest Comcast had previously sought to influence Sky News. However, she said this guarantee did not extend to ITV or ITN.

The Culture Secretary also raised concerns about how the merger would affect sports viewing. It is estimated that the combined company would control 60pc of all live linear sports viewing in the UK, far eclipsing the BBC.

Sky and ITV argue that the deal is necessary to give them the scale to compete with deep-pocketed rivals such as Netflix and Disney as audiences continue to move online.

They maintain that it would boost plurality by giving ITV the financial firepower to invest in journalism and compete for sports rights.

A Sky spokesman said: “We believe the transaction is in the public interest, with clear commitments already made to protect ITV’s identity, public service broadcasting obligations and the distinct editorial voices of Sky News and ITV News.”

An ITV spokesman said: “We look forward to cooperating fully with the CMA, DCMS and Ofcom in the review and will respond formally to the PIIN.”

data.title: Hire Tim Cook to lead Nvidia, Trump says
data.description:
Apple’s former chief executive should become the next boss of Nvidia after Jensen Huang’s resignation, Donald Trump has said.

The US president recommended Tim Cook, who led Apple for more than a decade, as Nvidia’s next chief executive after Mr Huang was brought down by his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and, allegedly, another with a colleague.

Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”

Shares in Nvidia, which makes semiconductor chips crucial to powering the AI boom, sank more than 14pc after Mr Huang announced his resignation on Thursday, wiping $600bn (£453bn) off its value.

Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday to discuss the chief executive’s future after reports that he had conducted a second affair, this time with an employee.

Hours after his resignation was announced, Reuters reported that Mr Huang had had a third affair, with another Nvidia employee.

It emerged last week that Mr Huang, who has been married for 41 years, had been in a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Ms Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and rented them out to Chinese AI firms, allowing them to use technology the US had banned from entering China.

Ms Huang is believed to have returned to China. Beijing has denied spying on Nvidia.

The chipmaker has lost nearly $1.6tn in market value since news of the relationship first emerged.

Allegations later emerged that Mr Huang had a second affair with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice-president of healthcare. Ms Powell has been contacted for comment.

Brian Mast, the Republican chairman of the House foreign affairs committee, said on Thursday that Mr Huang had agreed to testify before Congress within the next two weeks after several lawmakers had threatened to subpoena him.

Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, will take over as interim chief executive until a permanent replacement for Mr Huang is found. Nvidia has also appointed Harvey Jones, the former boss of semiconductor company Synopsys, as its first ever chairman.

‘Dark horse candidate’

Dan Ives, an analyst and partner at research firm Yorkville Ives, suggested Mr Cook would be a “dark horse candidate” considering the chequered history between the two companies.

Steve Jobs once accused Nvidia of copying technology from his other company, Pixar, which Nvidia denied.

The tech visionary also bristled when Huang refused to develop processors specifically for Mac computers.

Apple has largely avoided using Nvidia chips in its AI work, though the companies have occasionally collaborated more recently.

Mr Cook, 66, served as Apple’s chief operating officer from 2005, until becoming chief executive in 2011 after the death of co-founder Steve Jobs.

He continues to serve as the executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors.

Mr Cook is perhaps the only person besides Elon Musk with the experience of dealing with both President Trump and China. Both have also had strong relationships with Taiwan’s chip manufacturing industry.

Since Mr Trump returned to the White House, both Apple and Nvidia have enjoyed close ties to the president, with Mr Cook and Mr Huang appearing at a state dinner in September.

Mr Huang has been particularly close to the administration, which has relaxed export controls on certain AI chips produced by Nvidia.

During a trip to China earlier this year, Mr Trump had Air Force One make an extended stop at an Alaska air base so that the Nvidia founder could join the presidential party on its way to Beijing.

Mr Huang has frequently accompanied the US president at White House events and international missions, including the King’s state banquet last year.

Mr Trump said earlier this week that the FBI was “looking into” Mr Huang, but said he would stand by the embattled tech chief.

Nvidia’s board appeared to back him on Sunday, saying he would stay in his post while an investigation was carried out and that it had no evidence that national security had been compromised.

It did not issue an update on the investigation into Mr Huang on Thursday, or whether it would continue.

In the statement issued to investors, Nvidia said: “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”

The announcement did not include a statement from Mr Huang, who ran the business for 33 years after starting it in 1993. He will forfeit around $108m in unvested equity compensation after resigning from the company, although this translates to just 0.07pc of his total net worth.

The 63-year-old’s early bet on AI has turned Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies, with the industry dependent on the company’s microchips. The boom has also earned him a $145bn fortune, though the latest share price slump has reduced this to around $130bn, according to Bloomberg.

It is unclear what consequences Mr Huang could face if the board determines he has committed misconduct.

Stock exchange filings show the board is able to claw back pay if an executive is sacked for “cause”, which can include misconduct that results in material harm for the company.

Nvidia’s pay plan does not specify how far back this would go. Mr Huang was paid almost $400m in the last three years. The fact he officially resigned would also complicate matters.

Elizabeth Warren, a Democratic senator, said Mr Huang’s resignation did “not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws”.

‘Extraordinarily difficult period’

Nvidia had no clear succession plan or heir under Mr Huang, who maintained strict oversight of all elements of the company.

The company’s board said it would consider external candidates as a permanent successor to Mr Huang.

Ms Kress, his temporary replacement, joined Nvidia in 2013. Before that, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at tech giants including Cisco and Microsoft.

She said: “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

In a message to staff, Ms Kress acknowledged the situation as “an extraordinarily difficult period” for the company.

The email, seen by Reuters, said: “I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.

“The board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.”

Nvidia’s ‘rock star’ era is over

Mr Huang’s exit could have ripple effects across much of the tech industry. Mr Huang has channelled Nvidia’s huge profits into investments in many of the AI boom’s leading companies including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as financing a series of upstart companies buying his chips.

Stephanie Balaouras, of research firm Forrester, called Mr Huang’s resignation “a stress test for the AI boom”.

The news hammered shares in companies that enjoy close relationships with Nvidia. Data centre operators Coreweave and Nevis tumbled 4.5pc and 17pc respectively on Thursday.

Wall Street’s tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 plunged as much as 1.5pc in early trading, before recovering slightly to a 0.3pc fall at the closing bell.

Nivida shares closed down 4.3pc for the day.

The scandal could also lead to a US crackdown on Chinese companies accessing American technology.

Mr Ives said: “What seemed impossible a week ago is now a reality.

“The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past; his value to the company pre- and post this week is dramatically different.”

He added: “The board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.”

Mr Huang has a speculative route back into the business, with company bylaws allowing any shareholder with a stake of more than 3pc to nominate two directors at the company’s next annual meeting. This would then be voted on by shareholders.

The now former chief executive owns 3.6pc of the company, putting him above this threshold.

data.title: Drilling at Jackdaw in North Sea to start within days
data.description:
The controversial Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea is set to start production within days, an energy minister has said.

Michael Shanks, who is deputy to Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said gas from the site would start flowing into UK pipes shortly to help meet winter household energy demand.

He said: “We expect that in the coming days gas will start to flow from the field to meet demand right across Britain.”

Industry sources confirmed the timeline, although the exact date of “first gas” remains uncertain.

Adura, the joint venture between Shell and Equinor that owns Jackdaw, has repeatedly suggested production could ramp up from mid-November.

The gas from Jackdaw will travel through a 20-mile subsea pipeline to the Shearwater processing hub before coming ashore. Adura staff on Shearwater are said to be ready to open the taps.

It also emerged this week that offshore drilling rigs needed to prepare the platform for production have finished their work and departed, leaving the facility in apparent readiness. 

However, industry insiders suggest the switch-on may be delayed because of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey, where Ms Fahnbulleh is leading the UK delegation.

The arrival of Jackdaw’s gas in UK pipes will mark the culmination of a 21-year battle to get the field into production.

Discovered in 2005 in the central North Sea, Jackdaw used to belong to Shell, but after corporate restructuring it is now operated by the joint venture Adura.

It was granted a licence by ministers in June 2022 amid the European energy crisis triggered by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

However, the decision prompted a landmark legal case when Greenpeace successfully petitioned Scotland’s Court of Session, arguing that the Government had unlawfully ignored the climate impacts of burning Jackdaw’s gas.

Ms Fahnbulleh approved a fresh licence application last month.

The Government’s decision to approve Jackdaw has been controversial – flying in the face of Labour’s previous climate commitments and drawing criticism from Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary.

Mr Shanks, however, defended it strongly in a recent Westminster debate.

“The Jackdaw decision will support the country’s energy security, protecting hundreds of jobs and adding an estimated £2.9bn to the UK economy,” he said. “That decision was fully in line with our climate commitments.”

However, data have cast doubt on Mr Shanks’s claims.

At its peak, Jackdaw is projected to boost UK domestic gas production by approximately 6pc.

However, the North Sea accounts for only about 42pc of the UK’s gas needs, so Jackdaw’s contribution will be around 2.5pc of total UK gas supply – compensating for some of the decline in other fields.

The Jackdaw development coincides with new government data that show UK gas production fell by 7pc in the three months to June, hitting a near-record low, while net imports rose by 15pc.

Gas prices remain elevated at 230p per therm, compared with 82p a year ago.

An Adura spokesman said: “Jackdaw will provide an estimated 6pc of projected UK North Sea gas production – enough to heat the equivalent of 1.4 million homes – at peak production. This is a material contribution to Britain’s domestic energy supply and UK energy security.”

Adura is still awaiting a decision from Ms Fahnbulleh on the equally controversial Rosebank project west of Shetland, where it has invested £2bn in opening the UK’s largest remaining oil field.

data.title: Burnham has backed himself into a corner over public control of Thames Water
data.description:
The quest to save Thames Water is the saga with no end. Two and a half years after shareholders abandoned the company, its future is no more certain.

On the contrary, it is even more of a financial basket-case now than it was then, having been kept afloat by a steady drip-feed of emergency loans at a business that was already drowning in debt.

Additional borrowings since March 2024 stand at roughly £3bn with another £2.4bn on the cards, just to see it through the next 12 months.

That assumes, of course, that a disparate creditor base can agree on a deal – far from a foregone conclusion despite the high stakes.

The arrival of Andy Burnham in No 10 would bring an end to this financial purgatory, we were told.

Under Showtime Andy a privately led, debt-heavy industry ownership model that prioritised shareholder enrichment rather than customer care would be consigned to the dustbin, replaced by a system of greater “public control” – even though no one in Government has been able to explain what that means.

Burnham’s intervention has been characteristically cack-handed. Instead of steadying the ship, the Prime Minister has done precisely the opposite, exacerbating the uncertainty.

The problem is his propensity to speak first without thinking about the consequences. Just three months into his Premiership, a clear pattern has already been established: Burnham’s desire to be popular means he cannot help but put his foot in his mouth.

On Thames Water, he has backed himself into the tightest of corners. Burnham’s enthusiasm for nationalisation was such that it was widely assumed it would be among the first truly meaningful things the former mayor of Manchester would do upon setting foot in Downing Street.

The problem is that nobody in government, including the Prime Minister, paused to consider whether such a move was even plausible. Everyone was too concerned with playing to the gallery, telling an exasperated British public what it was assumed it wanted to hear.

But as ministers have quickly discovered, there is a big difference between wanting to do something and being able to, and the reality is that he inherited a country that cannot afford public ownership of critical assets such as Thames.

Some Labour figures have allowed themselves to be fooled into thinking that the Government could simply seize control without having to buy out the creditors.

But as has been pointed out, including in this column, such a move would amount to expropriation, something more associated with failing Communist regimes.

It’s fine to talk about wanting to end neoliberalism, but the reality is that the UK economy is massively reliant on foreign capital, much of it from long-term investors of the sort that had been lending to Thames long before the Wall Street hedge funds turned up.

Government contempt for the rule of law and property rights would be devastating to this country’s standing.

But even if Thames could be nationalised without recourse to the creditors, there is another glaring flaw that the pro-nationalisation crowd are unable to address: where will the investment come from afterwards?

There can be no doubt that water suppliers and their many shareholders are guilty of woeful underinvestment in the industry stretching back many years, something that a supine regulator must take some of the responsibility for.

But the country’s decrepit Victorian pipes and filthy waterways require a staggering £290bn of funding in the next 25 years just to ensure the taps stay on and our rivers are cleaned up.

These are figures from the National Audit Office, which also points out that at the current rate, it would take 700 years to renew the entire network.

Does this Government have that sort of money lying around? Of course not – not even close. It’s preposterous to even suggest that nationalisation of the water sector, or even just Thames, is somehow feasible.

Yet having seen his rhetoric collide with reality, the Prime Minister refuses to accept defeat. Officials are being told to come up with other ideas that would enable him to claim his promise of greater public control has been achieved.

The latest half-cocked plan supposedly on the table is to convert £100m of fines into a government stake, but a fag-packet calculation suggests that would equate to around 3pc of the company.

Not only is that close to meaningless, the creditors would still own the vast majority of it – something Labour MPs have made it clear they are vehemently opposed to.

It would also mean letting the company off a slew of fines for pollution when ministers have made a big song and dance about ensuring irresponsible water suppliers are properly held to account for any damage to the environment.

The result is a dangerous stalemate that will come back to bite the Prime Minister.

Burnham refuses to give his blessing to a restructuring proposal that’s been on the table for 18 months and will result in billions of pounds of Thames Water’s debts written off along with billions more in fresh equity pumped into the business.

Yet he and his team are yet to come up with any credible alternatives.

If the hedge funds aren’t the answer, and the Government doesn’t have a plan B, then what instead?

Wouldn’t a better solution be one in which the private sector continues to provide the vast financial resources required but under a regime of greater outside oversight and governance?

This can be done without the need for full nationalisation or for the state to have any economic interest at all.

Thames Water’s creditors have already agreed to a dividend freeze. They are willing to give the Government a golden share too, and the idea of allowing local mayors to have representation on its board has been floated too.

There could be an employee representative as well, which is the model in many European countries. Perhaps the privately held suppliers could also be partially floated on the stock exchange, a move that would guarantee much greater transparency and scrutiny.

There are many versions of this, but the Government urgently needs to clarify what its position is.

The longer Thames is left in limbo, the greater the risk that the vilified investors who have been propping it up will lose patience and walk away, leaving the Government to attempt to contain the fallout. This includes ensuring services aren’t interrupted.

If that happens, ministers will be responsible for one of the most spectacular slow-motion car crashes of all time.

data.title: Rayner on track to deliver fewer homes than the Tories
data.description:
Labour is on track to deliver fewer homes this parliament than the Conservatives in a setback for Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary.

A total of 1.14 million homes are expected to be added to Britain’s housing stock in the five years of this parliament, according to fresh forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

That is fewer than the nearly 1.18 million built in the 2019-24 parliament, which was cut short by an early election. The period of Conservative rule was also blighted by the pandemic lockdowns that shut down building sites.

The forecast from the OBR is a blow for Ms Rayner and Labour, which has made boosting housebuilding a key priority.

In its 2024 manifesto, Labour criticised the Conservatives for failing to build enough homes and promised to “get Britain building again”. The party vowed to deliver 1.5 million new homes over this parliament.

Industry has long warned that the Government is well off track to meet this goal but ministers have continued to defend it.

Ms Rayner described it as a “really difficult stretch target” in July but insisted the goal was not being dropped. In September, she admitted there was only a “slim chance” of building 1.5 million new homes but said: “I’m definitely not giving it up.”

The Housing Secretary has sought to blame the Iran war for blowing the Government off course, saying rising interest rates have weighed on the housing market.

However, Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, blamed the Government for the backwards step on home construction.

Ms Lam said: “Labour have no excuse. They’ve utterly failed to bring their pledge to fruition because they’ve layered taxes and red tape on to the industry, making building less and less viable.”

Steve Turner, the executive director of the Home Builders Federation, said Labour’s reforms since taking office were welcome but failed to address “the massive increase over the past 20 years in the level of taxation and policies, all with a cost, levied on to housebuilding by successive governments”.

These included requirements to build more affordable homes as well as environmental schemes and taxes, he said, adding that “demand is suppressed by a lack of affordable mortgage lending”.

The average five-year fixed mortgage currently available comes with an interest rate of almost 5.9pc, according to Moneyfacts, up from 4.9pc before the war in Iran began at the end of February.

John Healey, the Chancellor, has instructed Andrew Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, to seek more ways to help first-time buyers.

In a letter sent last week to set out the mandate of the Bank’s financial policy committee, Mr Healey called for the Bank to “target improving access to home ownership without prejudicing financial stability”, urging officials to look at rules around high loan-to-value mortgages.

Such mortgages are often taken by those buyers making their first step on to the housing ladder, requiring an initial loan which is relatively large compared to their earnings.

In forecasts produced alongside the Budget, the OBR cut its projection for house building during the coming five years by 190,000.

The watchdog said it still believed Labour’s reforms would “have a positive impact on housebuilding” but said the downgrade reflected “wider pressures in the construction sector because of weak demand, rising material costs and the impact of other regulatory changes”.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We’re getting this country building again and with new housing starts up 20pc compared to this time last year, and a 298pc increase in London alone, our bold planning reforms are working.

“We’ve always been clear that delivering 1.5 million homes was a stretch target and we recognise the challenges the sector is facing with construction costs and macro-economic headwinds.”

data.title: Two-tier safety regulations are strangling Britain’s housebuilding
data.description:
The Canada Water redevelopment plan is perhaps the most ambitious construction project in London. The first new London town in 50 years, it promises thousands of homes, millions of square feet of retail and office space, new streets and a town square.

The capital and the economy desperately need this sort of shot in the arm. But the scheme is now in deep trouble.

Rising costs, high inflation and interest rates, and weakening demand have put the second phase of the plans on hold, throwing the £3.6bn development into chaos.

You’ll see plenty of headlines blaming the economic weather, but there’s a truth that nobody wants to confront. The Canada Water scheme didn’t die by accident: it was killed off by government regulation.

The worsening housing market that dealt the coup de grâce was only the last of a series of blows, many of them dealt by government policy.

British Land has been trying to break ground in Canada Water since 2005, only for the financial crisis to hit the pause button. It was restarted in 2014, but it took six years for Phase 1 to begin. Such things take time, but lengthy consultation processes and wrangling held up the project until it had been shaken down for a massive 35pc “affordable housing” target.

Finally ready to go in 2020, Covid lockdowns caused matters to be delayed once again. And just as things went back to normal, in 2023, the Government brought in stringent new fire safety requirements that required the entire development to be redesigned.

The result was to further delay and reduce the viability of the project, leading the affordable housing target to be lowered to 9pc in a desperate last-ditch attempt to save the project.

Some of the new measures were sensible, but the most costly – and least rational – was the requirement for two stairwells in every structure above 18m.

This requirement made Britain an international outlier. In Europe and Asia, mid-rise apartments commonly have a single stairwell, and in France, Germany, Singapore, China and Sweden, the requirements only come in for buildings of around 50-60m, which would have covered a building the height of Grenfell in any case.

Indeed, we know that three central problematic features of the Grenfell disaster were nothing to do with the stairwell. The flammable cladding, of course, which is now rightly banned, allowed a fire to spread that would not have otherwise. A modern sprinkler system would have put out the fire in the first place but was absent. The fire doors would have given residents time to evacuate, but these failed because of poor maintenance by the council.

Beyond some minor adjustments to the cladding, none of these issues would have applied to Canada Water’s apartments, which, like all new high-rises, would have been equipped with sprinklers and brand new fire doors. A failure born entirely of the negligence of the state, and the age of Grenfell, is now being offloaded on to private developments.

In the US, there is emerging research which suggests that restrictive second stairwell requirements there have made construction more expensive and reduced floorspace, without demonstrably improving safety.

In fact, the British Government has done nothing to require existing high-rises to implement the most effective fire safety system – a sprinkler system (estimated to be 99pc effective by the London Fire Brigade) – while making it harder and more expensive to build the modern apartment blocks that would have them by default.

We’ve made new housing too safe to build. By loading excessive safety requirements on to new builds, we are slowing the roll-out of modern fire safety systems and trapping millions of people in unsafe, ageing buildings. It’s estimated that more than a million people live in apartments at risk of fire and as many as eight million live in homes that are in some way dangerous.

When we make it too costly to build safer homes by adding redundant safety measures, it’s those lives that we’re putting at risk.

data.title: Harvey Nichols’ former owner to sell London mansion for £40m
data.description:
The Hong Kong tycoon who formerly owned Harvey Nichols is to sell his London mansion for £40m to a parrot-fancying hedge fund boss.

Sir Dickson Poon, 70, has exchanged contracts for the sale of his Georgian townhouse in Belgrave Square, which sits in one of London’s most exclusive postcodes just a few hundred feet away from the grounds of Buckingham Palace.

It was bought by hedge fund manager Hamza Lemssouguer, according to the Financial Times.

The townhouse, which was sold off-market, was previously home to Queen Victoria’s grandson, Prince Arthur of Connaught, and was later used as the residence for East Africa’s high commissioner. The property’s current neighbours include the embassies of Germany and Norway.

Mr Lemssouguer is a former Credit Suisse trader who now runs his own firm, Arini Capital Management, which has made a name for itself by betting on distressed corporate debt.

He came to prominence after providing a loan to the Barclay family’s Very Group last year.

Away from finance, the Moroccan-born banker breeds parrots at his farm in Surrey, and has said that parrots are his passion.

Sir Dickson’s decision to sell comes as his empire is navigating a rough patch.

The Chinese magnate has been an influential figure in British retail since his company, Dickson Concepts, acquired Harvey Nichols from Burton Group in 1991 for £53m.

Nicknamed “Harvey Nicks”, and popularised in the television sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, the luxury London department store business expanded to other cities under Sir Dickson’s ownership and opened restaurants.

It now carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has more than 1,000 employees, with stores in Knightsbridge, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

However, Sir Dickson put the chain up for sale earlier this year amid mounting pressure on his business empire, with Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group acquiring it for an undisclosed sum.

Frasers said the brand was “a British institution with significant potential”, but faced “tough choices” to become sustainable again.

The deal includes the Harvey Nichols physical stores in the UK, international franchise partnerships and the company’s online presence.

Sir Dickson has stepped back from his former executive chairman duties after Dickson Concepts, which trades on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, warned that sales and profits were not likely to return to their historic growth rates.

Dickson Concepts has said the chain’s Hong Kong stores are unaffected.

Knight Frank, which was involved in the deal, was approached but declined to comment.

data.title: If only we all knew to say farewell as well as Monty Don
data.description:
It was a beautiful autumn day at Longmeadow last week: more like September than November. The Gardeners’ World camera came to rest on a striking purple-and-white dahlia, while down the garden path strode Monty Don carrying a tray of plants, his golden retriever Ned at his side.

The day may be autumn at its very best, said Monty, “but it can flatter to deceive. We know that winter is coming; we know that the cold, the rain and maybe even the snow will come, so it is worth making preparations for winter”.

Don read English at Cambridge, and his pronouncements on matters horticultural echo the rolling cadences of great men of letters of an earlier age: the garden-loving Elizabethan statesman, Sir Francis Bacon; or the orotund 17th-century polymath and author of The Garden of Cyrus, Sir Thomas Browne.

But as he introduced episode 32 of Gardeners’ World he knew, like most of his faithful audience, that it was farewell. After two decades presenting the show he was hanging up his presenter’s trowel. The only question was, how would he leave?

But first to matters horticultural, which looked forward, as you might expect, to spring. Monty’s tray of young plants turned out to contain Aquilegia alpina: hardy plants with exquisite blue flowers. The blue flower (as readers of Penelope Fitzgerald’s novel of that title will remember) is a symbol of unattainable happiness.

After various tasks, including planting a bulb lasagne, “the very first thing I ever did on television, back in 1989”, the moment arrived. Would there be the excruciating montage of Monty’s Best Bits that the Today programme is so fond of inflicting on its departing presenters?

There would not: Monty sat down, dog at his side, name-checked the departed hounds – Nigel, Nellie, Patti – then: “For the last time, bye-bye”. And off he went, back up the garden path, Ned at his side.

This is leaving done well: inexorable, without nostalgia, but with the tacit reassurance that he has taught us to manage without him. Mary Poppins left in similar fashion: blown away, umbrella aloft, on a changing wind, leaving the Banks household distraught but more resilient and magical than she found it.

The best partings are like this: sad but not hopeless, the chill of winter mitigated with the promise of renewal. Even Shakespeare’s tragedies eventually proffer a blue flower of some sort: the stage may be strewn with bodies but someone sensible, pragmatic, and possibly a touch dull, is poised to take over. (Speculation seethes as to who may inherit the Gardeners’ World crown.)

In art, as in gardening, the best stories come full circle. Hilary Mantel ended her Wolf Hall trilogy with a ghostly echo of the words that began Thomas Cromwell’s glittering rise to fortune: “So now get up.” It was, in a bleak way, consoling.

There have been many endings and near-endings in Monty Don’s career: “a broken heart, a broken spirit, a broken business” he recorded in his 2004 memoir, The Jewel Garden, jointly written with his wife, Sarah.

Now another ending: winter lies ahead (though the plants are confused and figs ripen on my tree, even as the leaves fall). In the garden, life slows but doesn’t stop: “The most exciting time of all,” Don concluded in The Jewel Garden, “is the shining here and now”.

data.title: People think I’m a mug for not moving to Monaco, says Phones 4u billionaire
data.description:
Despite spending most of the year in Monaco, John Caudwell continues to pay British taxes – even though he has very little faith in how the Treasury is spending the money.

“People think I’m a bit of a mug,” says the billionaire, who made his money founding Phones 4u. “I’m one of the very few people that live in Monaco and pay tax in the UK. Usually it’s the other way around.

“It would be the most natural thing in the world to move my tax residency there, and people think I’m crazy, not doing it.”

Caudwell, who says he is committed to Britain because of his patriotism, is one of the few onepercenters to speak out in favour of remaining a UK tax resident.

Many of Britain’s super-rich have quit the country since Labour ended the non-dom tax regime and raised inheritance taxes, moving to countries that offer tax breaks to wealthy global trotters such as Italy and Greece.

Caudwell says wealthy friends have been driven out by “hit” after “hit, hit, hit”, he says. “We’ve driven the people out and we’re not sucking the people in.”

The tycoon estimates he has handed the taxman some £400m since selling Phones 4u for £1.5bn in 2006. While he “can’t imagine” changing his tax residency, he warns his patience with Labour is running out.

“There’s only so much tolerance I’ve got,” he says. “I’m not going to ever say never, because I’m not going to sit and be throttled by a government that is not making things better for the people of Britain and then wants to take all my money off me.”

Caudwell, 74, has spent the last 15 years building 1 Mayfair, a £2bn complex he hopes will become the “world’s most prestigious apartment building”. We are speaking as he gives me a tour of the building, where apartments have just been put up for sale.

A lifelong Tory who switched his vote to Labour at the last election, the entrepreneur is betting that the world’s richest people still want a home in London, even as he questions his own decision to stay.

The grand entrance hall has a celestial hand-painted ceiling featuring Zodiac figures, based on the ancient Map of the Heavens on a huge copper plate in the Vatican Library collection in Rome. The design of the domed ceiling required the Vatican’s consent to reproduce. In the vestibule, the busts of four Roman emperors, Marcus Aurelius, Nero, Trajan and Augustus – look on.

“They’re all past caesars,” says Caudwell, who chose them for being “great builders of the Roman Empire”.

There is a fifth empty spot. “So I now become a new caesar of Mayfair,” he says, suggesting a bust of himself could occupy it. He’s only “half-joking”.

“I’m very proud of this building ... To have my brand on it is really quite important, because it is all about me.”

A closer look at the friezes in the grand reception shows his initials in the swirls, while a brass “C” sits on the balcony railings.

As well as a bust, Caudwell is also considering commissioning a marble statue of himself sitting on a wall in Audley Square, architectural plans in hand, and a bronze 15th century cavalier figure leaning over his shoulder to inspect them.

It may sound like the project is a monument to the entrepreneur’s ego. But Caudwell insists this is not about vanity. “I didn’t want to just introduce myself ... purely as an ego trip. I wanted it to be cool.”

Like the entrance hall, the building’s first show flat, priced at £83.7m with five bedrooms, is a study in maximalism. The walls are painted in an ombré fade that took 650 hours of labour, while the coffered ceiling, copied from Chatsworth House, cost up to 20 times as much as a flat one.

A chandelier is modelled on a diamond necklace worn by the Maharani of Kapurthala, a Hindu princess dubbed the Pearl of India who stayed at the Dorchester. The hotel, which is a two-minute walk away, will deploy its staff to provide residents with five-star services, earning a fee in the process.

The bedroom is apparently a nod to Marlene Dietrich’s pearls, with round lamps, pearls in the carpet, pearlescent wallpaper. The living room’s palette – dusky pinks and purples – is, according to Caudwell, an homage to Elizabeth Taylor. (Both Hollywood stars were also Dorchester guests.)

Caudwell jokes that whoever buys the flat will find its price tag the least of their worries, given the number of diamond necklaces needed to fill the jewellery drawers in the dressing room.

Prices start at £35m and will run up to £200m for the penthouse. When the whole complex is finished in 2027, it will feature a “crystal gallery” evoking the hall of mirrors in Versailles, a “billionaires’ library” and a spa with a 20-metre swimming pool.

But the timing is brutal. The top of London’s property market has been battered by stamp duty rises, surging borrowing costs and Labour’s looming mansion tax, as well as the end of the non-dom tax regime.

Data from Beauchamp Estates show that sales of new-build luxury flats in London have dropped by 87pc since 2023.

Nonetheless, Caudwell is confident. It’s “not a question of if they’ll sell, it’s only a question of when”, he insists. His team has whittled down 1,500 inquiries to 80 serious buyers, with eight viewings held in the next fortnight.

“There’s 4,000 multi-billionaires in the world,” says Caudwell. “If they want a London base as expensive as a £200m-plus penthouse apartment, a lot of them can afford it without even thinking about it.”

Caudwell estimates the project will be around £200m-£300m above budget, while his asking prices will sit at the level he set a decade ago. He admits there’ll be “not a lot of profit”.

“The profit would have been more, were London booming, and if Labour hadn’t made the decisions it did,” he added.

Does Caudwell regret switching his vote to Labour in 2024? He doesn’t but admits he is annoyed by “the mess Labour have made of the economy”.

He met ministers to discuss policies after Labour made business growth the crux of its manifesto. One suggestion he made was to hire a squad of business “ambassadors” working to woo leading technology companies to set up shop in the UK. “[It] would really change Britain’s prosperity,” he says.

Caudwell offered to do it himself a day a month for free. Sir Keir Starmer called it a “very interesting idea”, according to the Phones 4U founder.

“What did he do about it? After 18 months, nothing, and then he lost his job.” Caudwell adds: “They did ignore everything I said.”

Birmingham-born Caudwell, who left school at 16 to take up an engineering apprenticeship, dislikes Labour’s allusions to helping the “working people”, for overlooking the business owners “slogging their guts out morning, noon and night” to “keep the lights on”. “I know a lot of business people that are really offended by this talk of ‘working people’,” he says.

He is also scathing about Labour’s promise to annihilate red tape, and about John Healey’s Budget – likening it to moving “ashtrays” on the Titanic.

“If I ran my business the way the Government run the country, I would have been bankrupt before I started,” he says.

What the Government lacks, he argues, is the “dynamic and forceful” approach that Margaret Thatcher brought to public services.

Who will win his support at the next election? “Definitely not” Reform, given Nigel Farage’s enthusiasm for Donald Trump and scepticism on net zero. Caudwell, who describes himself as a humanitarian capitalist “slightly Right of centre”, says climate change is pushing the world into a “major catastrophe”.

For him, the Conservatives are the “only potential candidate”. He has met Kemi Badenoch and was “quite impressed”. He’s also “very much on the same page” as Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, on how to fix Britain’s problems.

The only sticking point is net zero, which Caudwell says should be a money-maker for Britain rather than a cost. Donating to the Tories again is a “faint possibility”.

He has donated just once before, giving £500,000 to the Conservative Party under Boris Johnson before the 2019 election. “I’ve only donated once in my life and that was to keep [then Labour leader Jeremy] Corbyn and [former shadow chancellor John] McDonnell out.”

“We’ve got two million unemployed, we’ve got one million Neets [people not in education, employment or training]. The cost to the economy and welfare state is colossal,” he adds.

“We’ve got to change all that, and we can’t change it by driving wealth out of the UK, by driving people away and by not bringing people in.”

Caudwell acknowledges these are views that are easy for a billionaire to express, but emphasises he is not “sitting here fattening my own war chest”, having pledged to give at least 70pc of his fortune to charity.

“I want Britain to be a great society, I want there to be more humanitarianism in the world, but I know how it has to be achieved.”

Surrounded by the opulence of 1 Mayfair, Caudwell insists Britain remains a great country if “somewhat spoiled by politics”. He will keep paying his dues, but it comes with a clear warning. “That’s not to say I’ll sit around and be a mug.”

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Police to crack down on 500 most prolific shoplifters
data.description:
Police will target 500 of the most prolific shoplifters in Britain with city centre bans and GPS tagging to track their movements.

Sixteen police forces will participate in a campaign where officers will use criminal behaviour orders to curb repeat offences by prolific shoplifters.

The court orders enable police to apply for restrictions banning convicted thieves from the specific areas in which they have focused their shoplifting. 

Officers can impose electronic tags to enforce the bans, as well as curfews and requirements to undergo treatment for drug or drink addiction.

The criminal behaviour orders can also be used to ban offenders from meeting or gathering with named individuals, possessing alcohol in public, using social media or digital contact, and carrying or using certain articles such as e-bikes, tools or spray paint cans.

Breaches of the orders carry a maximum penalty of five years in jail.

Just 10 per cent of shoplifters are responsible for 70 per cent of store thefts in Britain, according to research by Auror, a data-sharing platform that enables retailers such as M&S, Tesco and Boots, as well as police, to identify prolific offenders.

‘Wreaking havoc on high streets’

Similar data analysed by the Metropolitan Police found that 104 prolific shoplifters were responsible for 4,389 offences in the past two years, a third of all store thefts in London for which a suspect had been identified.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, said: “A small number of offenders commit a disproportionate amount of shop theft. They wreak havoc on our high streets, leave businesses out of pocket and make retail workers scared to go to work.

“Under this Government, shop theft is starting to fall, and more offenders are getting charged. Now we are going further by targeting those who are causing so much harm to our communities and stopping them in their tracks.”

Retail chiefs say thieves have become “more brazen, more organised and more aggressive” amid a fourfold increase in shoplifting since the Covid pandemic.

It has risen to record highs of more than 500,000 offences a year in England and Wales, although the British Retail Consortium estimates under-reporting means there are in reality some 5.5m store thefts in a year, resulting in direct losses of £2.2bn.

That means the top 10 per cent of prolific offenders could be responsible for as many as 3.8m thefts at a cost of £1.4bn a year.

However, thefts have started to plateau, with data published by Auror showing that violence by shoplifters in stores has fallen by up to 20 per cent since police and shops started targeting prolific offenders.

Under the trial scheme, police, probation and other partners will work from a single, personalised plan for each individual shoplifter to build stronger cases for the courts by gathering evidence of multiple offences.

Tackling repeat offenders is proven to make a dramatic difference to overall crime levels. According to Met Police data, Operation Kelleher, a crackdown targeting prolific offenders in Bromley last year, reduced recorded retail crime by 70 per cent. Shops reported stock losses down by as much as 80 per cent.

The operation targeted 10 prolific offenders, leading to arrests and charges, with criminal behaviour orders secured against several offenders. One shop saw its weekly losses fall from £7,000 to £400.

An initial £2.5m in funding will be available to the 16 forces taking part in the new scheme: Avon and Somerset Police, Devon and Cornwall Police, Essex Police, Greater Manchester Police, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, Merseyside Police, Metropolitan Police Service, Northumbria Police, North Yorkshire Police, Nottinghamshire Police, South Yorkshire Police, Suffolk Police, Sussex Police, Thames Valley Police, West Midlands Police and West Yorkshire Police.

Simon Roberts, the chief executive of Sainsbury’s, said: “Retail crime is a national emergency, which requires a national response, and targeted action from government and police against the prolific offenders who repeatedly target stores is an important step forward.

“We now need to see more arrests and prosecutions of those who target UK retailers without fear of consequences and we look forward to working closely with authorities as these measures are put into action.”

data.title: Janet Malcolm, the finest – and most hated – journalist in town
data.description:
Among discerning members of the literati, Janet Malcolm is treated with reverence. A long-time New Yorker journalist, serving for 58 years until her death in 2021, she’s admired for her exacting prose and her shrewd analysis. Yet her aversion to the cult-of-personality style of journalism, which put the writer at the centre, meant she was never quite a celebrity.

I came to know Malcolm’s work after I’d been working as a journalist for a few years. Other writers, a bit older and much cleverer than me, recommended her. I was so taken with the combination of her subjects and her meticulous style – never dry, never florid – that I soon arranged a weekend break in a coastal B&B, taking nothing but all of her books.

Why is Malcolm so intriguing? Firstly, her work. She wrote for The New Yorker first as a lifestyle journalist, then a photography critic, and eventually as a general staff writer. In the last of those roles, she undertook in-depth profiles, literary criticism and longer-form investigations on a sequence of related subjects: psychoanalysis, a heated dispute about Freud’s legacy, the moral question of what journalists should disclose to their subjects, the ethics of biography as seen through Sylvia Plath’s story, a murder-for-hire case in a religious community and plenty more.

One of Malcolm’s great gifts was to be constantly and curiously aware of what her presence as a journalist was doing to the subject and the situation. She never, though, clumsily foregrounded her own experience. Each subject she took on was interesting not only in its own right but in a second light: how does this subject morph under my gaze? I have no especial interest in photography or visual art, but I read her writing on those topics with as much thirst as I did that on subjects more in my wheelhouse (psychoanalysis, Sylvia Plath).

Secondly, the woman herself. She defied aestheticisation, as many of her peers did not. At the opening of The Absent Woman, a nimble and tender new biography of Malcolm, Eve Sneider tells us that in 2014, when both Malcolm and her fellow essayist Joan Didion were turning 80, New York magazine asked to run a joint feature in tribute. Malcolm declined. Her work is light on emotional or personal news. (Didion, by contrast, modelled for Celine in her latter years, and never shied away from the impulse among some of her fans to enshrine her as a cultural icon.) There’s something valuable in Malcolm’s caution against being too personally available: something always tantalisingly withheld. She reminds us, I think, of the pleasure of ephemera, especially in an age when it’s becoming extinct.

She was born Jana Klara Wienerová in 1934, in Prague, to a family of Jewish intellectuals. In 1939, they fled to America to avoid Nazi persecution, and settled in Manhattan, in a heavily Central and Eastern European neighbourhood. Their Jewishness was, understandably, a matter of anxiety. Janet’s father, Joseph, changed the family name to “Winn”; he and his wife, Hanna, decided not to disclose their religion to the children.

The family assimilated well, though complicatedly so: both Jewishness and European identity would remain sensitive for Malcolm’s sense of self. While she would wrestle with and to some degree bury her heritage, she would also end up surrounded in her adult life by people who had the same sensibilities. “A select few called her ‘Jana’, including Philip Roth,” Sneider writes. “They traded notes on each other’s writing, they gossiped, they cracked jokes.” (At one point, when a Malcolm essay was being praised from all quarters, he wrote a note to her: “There is a devil in you called Jana and she should be encouraged, prodded, rewarded, at every turn.”)

Malcolm was among the first generation of writers who grew up reading The New Yorker. She attended the University of Michigan, graduated in 1955 and – following her husband Donald, who’d been hired already – was taken on by the magazine. Her beginnings were in gift guides, then photography columns, but in 1978 she published her first piece on psychoanalysis, a subject that would become the undercurrent of her career.

First came Psychoanalysis: The Impossible Profession in 1981, a book widely feted both in literary circles and among the profession she sought to illuminate. Analysis was, back then, in a slump, fearful of its dwindling cultural significance; here was a sharp reinvigoration. Malcolm is unmistakably everywhere, through the mordant wit of her observation. She tells one loquacious analyst that she gets sick of listening to him talk without being able to respond. Doesn’t he get sick of listening to his patients? “And how!” he responds with glee.

After the success of that book came In the Freud Archives in 1984, equally brilliant and riveting – but also the genesis of a traumatic, lengthy legal battle with one of its subjects. Malcolm depicts a power struggle between the analysts Jeffrey Masson and Kurt Eissler over Freud’s legacy and who would be granted access to the archive of the great man. It’s a moreish tale of competing egos and ideas, of men of a certain stature who pride themselves on having insights into the human condition yet can’t see their own silliness. As Sneider reports, one admiring reader told Malcolm: “You are, if I may say, an inspired gossip.”

This book and its aftermath would prove a fulcrum for Malcolm’s career. Masson, in particular, had been an incautious and flamboyant respondent, bragging about his womanising proclivities as well as his analytic genius, and he now took Malcolm to court alleging defamation, citing several remarks attributed to him that Malcolm didn’t have on tape. Sneider’s account of the trial is absorbing. As Malcolm herself knew, there’s nothing like a trial to distil vast, abstract questions in compellingly strange and human ways. She was cleared in 1994 – after a jury found that she’d intended no malice, even if the quotes had been fabricated – but the ordeal had roused plenty of professional animosity among fellow journalists, who disdained what they perceived as Malcolm’s hubris and hypocrisy.

The lengthy legal battle had flown under the radar for some years, but as it rumbled on Malcolm had published another pair of New Yorker pieces in 1989 that would become a classic book: The Journalist and the Murderer. That story took as its subject a lawsuit between a non-fiction writer named Joe McGinniss and a man convicted of murder, Jeffrey Macdonald. McGinniss had been hired to write about Macdonald’s trial. He had feigned sympathy and belief in Macdonald’s innocence to gain his trust and proximity, before publishing a book that portrayed the other man as an egotistical killer. An appalled Macdonald sued, accusing McGinniss of fraud; they eventually reached a financial settlement. It was an almost too perfect iteration of the questions about loyalty and disclosure with which Malcolm was obsessed.

But the book functioned, in many ways, as a brutal criticism of the profession of journalism itself. Her colleagues in the industry were furious. She didn’t mention her own ongoing legal troubles – she was herself, after all, a journalist accused of defamation – even as she pored over the alleged offences of others. This was too much for some to take. In New York magazine, John Taylor wrote a feature titled Holier Than Thou: The Curious Case of the Ferocious New Yorker Article, in which he and various subjects of Malcolm’s theorised that The Journalist and the Murderer served as a way for Malcolm to launder guilt about her own misdoings. Sneider is excellent at conveying the hubbub of Malcolm’s salivating colleagues, eager to decry her throughout these years.

The New York Times and New York, in particular, showed Malcolm open contempt. Today, it’s shocking to read: much of their disgust was over her appearance and demeanour. In the Times: “Ms Malcolm’s severe bearing and slight accent hark back to her European childhood.” In New York: “Her dark, lank hair is parted in the center… which has the effect, along with her owlishly oversized glasses, of emphasising her broad Slavic cheeks.” She was held up as smug and superior, and The New Yorker was implicated alongside her.

But, as widely reviled as she was in that period, Malcolm has come to be known, 30 years on, as a journalist’s journalist. Her most famous line, the beginning of The Journalist and the Murderer, is: “Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is morally indefensible.” My boyfriend, who works as an editor on The New Yorker, winces when this line arises in conversation, the gist of his objection being: great line, obviously untrue exaggeration. I was pleased to show him a passage from Sneider’s book, showing that some of Malcolm’s other drafts had the journalist “aware” rather than “know”-ing, and not judged as “morally indefensible” but the more nuanced “obscurely shameful”. Part of the pleasure in reading Sneider’s biography is in having these famous sentences revealed in the fullness of their process: the care and time from which they benefitted.

Malcolm reverted to her original, sturdier proclamation upon her daughter’s advice. Again, it provoked her peers. One has to admire Malcolm’s willingness to be an irritant even as she fought legal battles and professional eschewment. Today, her line is quoted admiringly, the book taught in journalism schools. And Malcolm’s not-niceness is seen now for what it always was: a restless genius for observation, for being precise.

★★★★★

The Absent Woman is published by Atlantic at £18.99. To order your copy, call 0330 173 0523 or visit Telegraph Books

data.title: Towering wall that blocked homeowner’s sea view removed
data.description:
A 16ft wall that blocked a homeowner’s sea view has been removed after a 14-month row.

Liz Bates said the value of her home in Bournemouth, Dorset, fell by an estimated £50,000 because the wall obstructed her view.

The wall screened a rooftop terrace on a flat being built in a neighbouring block but it did not have planning permission.

Planning inspectors ruled three months ago that it had a “harmful overbearing impact” on Mrs Bates’s home and the size of the roof terrace “far exceeded what could be reasonably described as modest”.

However, instead of admitting defeat and demolishing the wall, Eddie Fitzsimmons, the developer, submitted an application to replace the brick wall with an opaque glass screen.

Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP) council rejected the plans.

Builders have taken down the wall – which was erected in September 2025 – leaving temporary scaffolding in its place.

Mrs Bates said: “I want to say I’m really happy, but I fear they will still come back in a couple of months [with another application].”

The 43-year-old is one of about 100 residents who have claimed their lives have been “ruined” by the development of four cliff-top apartment blocks of 27 flats in front of their homes in the affluent Southbourne area of Bournemouth.

Mrs Bates argued the roof terrace would be big enough to stage large outdoor parties and the screen would do nothing to stop noise and smells drifting into her house.

In its latest application, Mr Fitzsimmons’ Vivir Estates company said the shortened roof terrace would not be big enough to host parties, and the glass screen would “not result in an overbearing impact” upon Mrs Bates’s home.

Chris Miell, of Pure Town Planning, who represented the developer, told the council’s planning committee: “The inspector’s decision specified the roof terrace as it was previously proposed. It doesn’t mean that any roof terrace is unacceptable at this site.

“It would not cause material harm to the living conditions of neighbouring properties and overcomes the planning inspector’s concerns.”

The two and four-storey blocks in the main development are being built on a former council car park in front of 24 existing properties.

BCP council put the Southbourne Crossroads car park site up for sale in 2017 when it was underused, and denied two planning applications for the site.

The local authority was overruled after an appeal from Vivir Estates.

Labour has been accused of giving rail union activists a “blank cheque” to campaign during work hours.

Groups including the RMT, the Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association and the Aslef train drivers’ association will be allowed to carry out trade union work while being paid as if they were in their day jobs.

Keir Mather, a junior minister, said that the Department for Transport (DfT)’s passenger train agency, DfT Operator, had signed a “voluntary recognition agreement” with the three main rail unions.

That agreement, the minister said, had no limits on taxpayer funding of trade union activism during normal working hours. The funding will be supplied via Great British Railways, the planned state body unifying the rail network.

Richard Holden MP, the shadow transport secretary, said: “It’s crystal clear that Andy Burnham’s Labour Government is repeating Keir Starmer’s mistakes and giving a blank cheque to their trades union paymasters on the trains – this time with so called ‘facility time’ which, in reality, means political campaigning at the expense of passengers and taxpayers.

“Rather than raising taxes and fares to pay for union activity, the Government should be concentrating on making railways cheaper, safer and more reliable for passengers and taxpayers,” the Conservative MP added.

“Sadly under Labour, serving the unions rather than the public will always be their top priority.”

Union sources say that facility time consists of up to 50 per cent of a worker’s normal contracted hours which can be spent performing activities such as identifying health and safety problems or dealing with workplace disciplinary problems.

This is claimed to save employers money by avoiding the need to hire more HR staff.

Previously, under the Civil Service’s wider Facility Time Framework document, government departments were not allowed to spend more than 0.1 per cent of their annual salary bill on trade union activists’ facility time.

This would have limited DfT and its agencies, such as DfT Operator or the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, to a maximum of about £58,000 per year being spent on facility time.

But Mr Mather confirmed that all limits have been lifted. In a parliamentary response to a question posed by Mr Holden, he said: “The [trade union] agreement does not prescribe a fixed facility time entitlement, budget or payroll percentage.

“Instead, reasonable paid time off for accredited representatives will be managed in line with legislation, Acas guidance and operational requirements.

“As facility time will vary according to operational need and levels of trade union activity, it is not currently possible to provide a reliable estimate of its annual cost or proportion of payroll,” he added, saying that such paid time off “will be managed proportionately, balancing statutory obligations, operational delivery and value for money considerations”.

Facility time includes activities such as attending union conferences during working hours, as well as “union facing” projects such as branch meetings.

Critics have said Labour’s watering down of rules ensuring that public sector union members are not paid for non-work activities during work time effectively channels cash into the unions’ pockets.

Trade unions fund the Labour Party and individual Labour MPs to the tune of millions of pounds per year.

Key taxpayer protections against union misuse of facility time were torn up by Sir Keir Starmer’s government, including laws ensuring departments revealed how much facility time was granted to union activists.

Labour also weakened transparency laws around trade union financing, making it harder for the public to understand and scrutinise how much money unions are pouring into political donations, as well as identifying the sources and targets of that funding.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “Any suggestion that these arrangements provide a blank cheque for facility time is wrong.

“The voluntary recognition agreement that DfT Operator has reached applies only to union representation for a small number of predominantly former DfT employees who transferred into DfT Operator and does not extend to the whole industry.

“We are taking a pragmatic approach that reflects established industrial relations practice and means workplace issues can be dealt with constructively.”

The spokesman also denied that the agreement applied to DFT Operator staff who were members of the RMT, TSSA or Aslef unions, without giving further detail.

data.title: Banks ban AI from accounts over fears of rogue agents
data.description:
Britain’s biggest banks have banned AI agents from accessing customer accounts over fears that personal finance bots will go rogue.

HSBC, Nationwide, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds have all moved to block AI agents, including in some cases specific bans on making transactions on a customer’s behalf without their direct involvement.

AI agents that can manage people’s money – and their personal lives – are seen as one of the most promising frontiers for the technology.

However, banks are concerned that bots could go rogue and mismanage people’s money, with no clear rules as to who would be responsible in that scenario. Lenders are also concerned that en masse, bot-enabled switches could also threaten profits and, in a worst-case scenario, financial stability.

In September, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched Muse, a personal AI assistant that can carry out tasks such as shopping and managing bills for users. The app, which has not yet launched in the UK but is expected to, has topped download charts in North America.

Rather than just providing advice, AI agents such as Muse will carry out tasks such as sending emails or ordering shopping. Increasingly in the US, customers are directing their agents to manage their savings directly in their bank accounts.

Similar products are expected in Britain. Anne Boden, the founder of Starling Bank, has argued that AI should be entrusted with people’s finances and recently announced on LinkedIn that she was hiring engineers for a new startup which would be “right at the start of the next revolution in banking technology”.

Bank bosses are concerned that bots could go rogue, following a series of incidents outside the financial system in which AI has accessed systems without authorisation.

Manus Costello, the chief financial officer at Standard Chartered, said last week: “We need to be very careful that those tools are safe for customers and safe for us before we allow them in.”

Will Chalmers, the chief financial officer of Lloyds, said recently the bank had not seen any sign of AI agents accessing bank accounts but added: “We do guard against that type of risk, and we take it very seriously.”

The Financial Conduct Authority is working with the City and other regulators to develop rules to govern AI agents in finance.

Sources close to the regulator said it was up to the banks to make decisions on AI access but added that early research showed that agents could behave in unexpected ways.

The bans from UK banks are understood to be pre-emptive, with no signs yet that AI bots are accessing accounts.

As well as concerns about rogue AI, the technology also poses a potential threat to banks.

McKinsey has warned that savers could shift up to £700bn out of accounts that offer little or no returns and into savings products on the advice of AI chatbots.

If just 5pc to 10pc of bank balances are moved this way, the profits lenders make on deposits could drop by a fifth or more.

Anthropic and OpenAI both recently launched personal finance products that plug in to people’s accounts and give them advice on what to do with their money. However, the services only read financial information, rather than taking action on users’ behalf.

‘You don’t want rogue agents’

There are also fears that AI agents acting in unison could pull deposits from a bank at the same moment, triggering a run at machine speed.

Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan, warned earlier this year: “It’s a new world and with all these bots and agents, could someone ... cause a problem? Maybe.”

The bans by British banks follow similar moves in the US and Canada, where Citigroup, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and JP Morgan have all blocked AI agents from accessing accounts.

“You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” Mr Dimon said during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call.

Rick Wurster, the chief executive of Charles Schwab, the US brokerage giant, said that the company was actively blocking between 10 and 20 clients a week from using AI agents.

“We don’t want someone just giving their password to Muse, and letting Muse come in and take action on that client’s behalf,” Mr Wurster said in a recent interview. “We can’t control it, the client can’t control it, something could go wrong and who’s liable?”

AI agents face tougher guardrails in the UK, where strict authentication rules mean most payments must be approved through a mobile banking app, often with a fingerprint or face scan.

data.title: Water bosses lose bonuses after worst pollution on record
data.description:
Several water bosses will be blocked from receiving bonuses after their companies were awarded the worst possible environmental rating.

One-star ratings at Southern Water, Thames Water, South West Water and Yorkshire Water were all confirmed by the Environment Agency on Thursday.

This means they will now be blocked from paying executive bonuses as part of a government crackdown launched last year that seeks to prevent companies rewarding failure.

The latest ratings were confirmed as part of the agency’s annual performance review. The best possible rating is four stars, which was only achieved by Severn Trent.

The agency announced on Thursday that pollution incidents are still far too high across the UK, with six category 1 incidents reported in 2025.

These are incidents deemed to have had a major effect on the environment or on households, and also lead to a ban on bonuses.

Both Severn Trent and Anglian Water were found liable for category 1 incidents in 2025, meaning they will also be barred from handing payouts to their bosses.

Overall, the EA found that there were 74 serious sewage pollution incidents in 2025, only slightly fewer than the 75 in 2024.

Alan Lovell, the chairman of the Environment Agency, said that the companies awarded one-star ratings had fallen “well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public”.

Ministers are now set to visit a number of sites to interrogate companies’ performance.

Dame Angela Eagle, the Environment Secretary, said she will also be looking at options to strengthen the ban on executives’ bonuses.

It follows the first ever joint report from the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales, the Drinking Water Inspectorate and Ofwat, which leaves nowhere for underperforming companies to hide.

In total, there were 2,666 sewage and water supply incidents that took place in 2025, with Thames Water responsible for more than any other supplier: 464.

That was down from 2,801 in 2024.

James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action, said: “Another year, another record low.

“In 2025 almost every water company in England has been ranked as performing poorly, and the sewage kept flowing into our rivers just as it has done for years.

“This year’s figures show that performance is getting worse, not better.”

PM vows to introduce more ‘public control’

Mr Wallace said the latest pollution figures are further evidence that Thames Water, which released 108,000 hours of raw sewage into Britain’s waterways last year, should be put into special administration.

The latest pollution failures have emerged despite £5bn of investment from water companies, which has pushed households’ bills.

The figures come at a critical moment for the water industry after Andy Burnham vowed to introduce more “public control” over the sector.

A spokesman for Water UK, which represents the sector, admitted that improvements were needed.

He said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.”

Dame Angela said: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and branch reform cannot wait.

“People are sick of excuses. I am demanding answer from the companies that are failing.”
