data.title: Norway is all the proof we need that Rosebank must be approved
data.description:
It was great to read this week about how well one of the major players in the North Sea is doing, and how much the whole country is benefiting from its success. Output is booming, it has reported its strongest profits in four years, plenty of skilled jobs are being created, and the government is raking in hundreds of millions in extra revenue both as a shareholder, and, of course, from all the taxes it pays.

There is just one catch. The company is Norway’s Equinor, and it is our Scandinavian neighbours who are benefitting from its success.

The Norwegian giant is a template for how we could be managing our own energy resources – if only our political leaders stopped dithering and had the sense to follow its lead.

Equinor reported another strong set of results this week. Its earnings before tax for the third quarter doubled to $12.4​bn (£9.3bn) from $6.2bn, the highest level since 2022. Production is up, and its pipeline is strong.

“The basis for this result is, of course, that we have increased production and, ​just as importantly, that prices have risen significantly,” according to Anders Opedal, its chief executive. Indeed, there is plenty more where that came from. On Thursday the company announced that estimates of the amount of recoverable gas in its Afrodite field were more than double the earlier estimates. It will be keeping the pipelines full for many years to come.

Given all that, it is no great surprise that its shares are up by 86pc so far this year, and keep hitting all time highs. The Norwegian government owns 67pc of the company, so at a rough estimate it has made more than £20bn this year alone from its shareholding. 

On top of that it has collected corporation tax, as well as the petroleum taxes which, when taken together, means the government takes in more than 70pc of any profits made by its energy giants. In short, it is not just that the company is doing well. So is the whole country. Indeed, all the money Equinor is generating helps explain why Norway has a huge budget surplus and has been cutting taxes.

The contrast with Britain could hardly be more painful. While a company such as Equinor is booming on the back of strong oil and gas prices and rising production, we have been running down our own resources.

Equinor itself has always been a major player in the fields off the Aberdeen coast, but only last month it repeated that a combination of punishing taxes and activist-led lawfare meant the industry was “uninvestable”.

Overall North Sea production has been in steady decline for years, and all the so-called renewable experts keep telling us that it is pointless to think about preserving it because there is hardly any oil and gas left in its exhausted fields, and even if there were it wouldn’t make any difference to the global price. Even leaving aside our “global leadership” on combatting climate change there isn’t any money to be made.

The Norwegian example tells that is not, to be put it politely, quite the whole story. We have, in fairness, taken one tiny baby step towards boosting production again in the British section of the North Sea.

After years of tortured delays the Jackdaw gas field has finally been approved. But we are still waiting on a final decision on the Rosebank field, even though, bizarrely, both the Chancellor and the Office for Budget Responsibility have already pencilled in the tax revenues that will start flowing once it starts production. Apparently it is still being held up while Labour’s boneheaded backbenches fight a rearguard action to try to delay it all over again.

That is simply not good enough. There is no reason not to approve the field immediately. Dithering and delaying doesn’t help the workers in Aberdeen who need jobs, it doesn’t help a Treasury that needs the money, and it doesn’t even help the climate, given that we just import fossil fuels instead. All it does is reinforce the impression across the energy industry that Britain is no longer a serious country, and not one worth wasting time and money on. and money on.

Our approvals should not stop with just those two fields, there is so much more that we could be doing. Offshore Energies UK has identified more than 100 projects in the North Sea that we could be exploiting, while the Norwegian experience tells us that once you start drilling, and using the latest techniques, there is always more energy locked up in the ground than initially expected.

In reality, Equinor is a role model for how to manage the North Sea while gradually transitioning to wind, solar and nuclear power. Extend the life of existing fields for as long as you can and develop new ones where possible.

Tax the industry so the Government makes plenty of money, but not at such a high rate that it is impossible for the companies investing their capital to make a decent return or to reward their shareholders for the risks they are taking. And, if possible, take a significant government stake in the main exploration and development company so that the state benefits as a shareholder and doesn’t have any incentive to punish the operators with sky high taxes. It is hardly complicated stuff.

All we need are the political leaders with the basic intellectual curiosity to take a look at something that is working really well for a close neighbour, and one with almost exactly the same geographic resources we have. Given the track record of this Government, we won’t hold our breath – but the template is right there in front of us.

data.title: Starling flies into trouble after bank’s wings clipped
data.description:
When Anne Boden, the founder of Starling Bank, published a book chronicling how she set up Britain’s first digital-only bank, she subtitled it How I Disrupted an Industry.

Six years after that book was published, it is Starling itself that is being disrupted.

Boden is long gone and has sold her final stake in the business this year at a valuation of only £1.7bn — less than half the £4bn valuation it was said to be targeting last year.

Now Raman Bhatia, who replaced Boden as Starling’s chief executive, is now heading for the exit after just two years in the role.

His departure follows a large number of the bank’s board members over the last year, some of whom reportedly had disagreements with Starling’s largest shareholder, Harald McPike.

And the bank is still subject to restrictions imposed by the City watchdog that have clipped its wings and left it struggling to grow.

The upheaval comes even as rivals start to pull away. Revolut recently completed a fundraising round at a valuation of $115bn (£87bn). Monzo, founded by Tom Blomfield, a former Starling Bank employee, is reportedly in talks to raise money at a £7bn valuation.

With Starling lagging, the City is alive with speculation about what might happen to the lender. McPike, a Bahamas-based Austrian billionaire who owns 37.5pc of the bank, is said to have lost interest in a London stock market listing. Could a deal with the likes of Monzo or another bank be on the cards?

Boden, a Welsh former executive of Allied Irish Banks, founded Starling in 2014 as a bank tailored for smartphones.

Government policy changes intended to encourage competition in banking gave rise to several rivals but Starling Bank always positioned itself as a more mature business than the competitors nipping at its heels, thanks in part to Ms Boden’s banking pedigree.

Boden said it was “pulling away from the rest of the Fintech pack” in 2021 after it reported a 600pc rise in revenue to £97.6m.

But the announcement proved a high point for the bank. Roughly two months later, the City watchdog banned Starling from onboarding higher-risk customers, and it was fined £29m in 2024 for “shockingly lax” controls around risky customers. Restrictions remain in place today.

Separately, Starling Bank had distributed £1.6bn in UK Bounce Back Loans (BBLS) during the Covid-19 pandemic. The government-guaranteed loans were intended to support business during the pandemic but later faced scrutiny over weak fraud-checks and non-compliant loans. Restrictions remain in place today.

Boden departed the bank in 2024 to focus on developing a new AI business and recently announced on LinkedIn that she was hiring engineers for a new startup that would be “right at the start of the next revolution in banking technology”.

While Boden has moved on, the bank she founded is still searching for direction.

In December 2025, Bhatia said Starling was exploring applying for a US banking licence. However, by April, Declan Ferguson, the company’s chief financial officer, said that it was not seeking a licence and would instead pursue a “more modest acquisition” focused on business-to-business products, not retail. (Ferguson is seen as a front-runner to replace Bhatia.)

Questions over US expansion are also overshadowing Engine, a part of Starling that sells its banking technology to other lenders.

It is regarded as a key driver of potential future growth. However, since it launched as a separate business in 2022, Engine has signed up only four clients and is yet to acquire a US customer, even though it opened a New York office in 2025 and hired Deloitte and PwC to find prospects.

Its current customers include banks from Romania, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, but it hasn’t announced a new client since February.

Meanwhile, Starling’s UK bank – its core business – is finding it harder to compete for customers.

In its latest accounts for the 12 months to March, Starling reported a 5pc increase in deposits to £12.7bn, but all of its growth came from a 45pc increase in savings-account deposits.

Personal current-account balances fell 6pc, eroding its cheapest form of funding and leaving it more exposed as rates fall. In a recent bond offering, it warned that a faster-than-expected fall in rates “could present a threat to the group’s earnings and profitability”.

Rupert Ghose, an adviser to fintech companies and a former financial research analyst, said Boden “used to say, ‘We may not just chase customer numbers, but we’re going to get deposits, which is the heart of traditional banking, and we’re going to make money on the deposits.’And they never really did that. And they haven’t done the other stuff the young cool kids did”.

The bank, which has a sponsorship deal with Arsenal FC, has 4.9 million UK accounts, of which about 500,000 are businesses. By comparison, Monzo has more than 15 million customers.

As it faces increasing competition for deposits, Starling is pushing into lending. Mortgages makeup 95pc of its loan book and it bought Fleet Mortgages, a buy-to-let lender, for £50m in July 2021. Starling purchased a £230m unsecured consumer loan book in May.

The bank is also exploring buying mainstream unsecured lenders, non-bank lenders and specialist owner-occupied mortgage lenders.

With Starling seemingly fighting harder to stand still, the bank has become a takeover target. Last year, Shawbrook, the specialist lender, made a tentative approach about a merger that would have created a combined group worth about £5bn.

A potential combination with one of Britain’s many specialist banks – or larger fintechs – has also been the subject of much discussion in the City. Ghose recently suggested that Monzo might make a potential partner.

“Investment bankers have got nothing else to do. There’s no IPOs in the UK ... They might as well go around to Monzo and Starling and hatch it out and merge the two,” he said.

“Starling’s making a couple of hundred million in profit. Monzo is actually not making much profit. You put the two together ... I just think the cost savings would be significant. I think you’d get scale.”

Its backers insist the business is worth far more than the £1.7bn implied by Boden’s recent transaction. Chrysalis, the investment trust that owns about 12pc of Starling and is winding down its portfolio, wrote up its stake last week to a level Jefferies said implied a £3.4bn valuation.

But even Jefferies’ analysts said the route to cashing in “is still unclear”. For a bank that once cast itself as the adult at the table, the next chief executive’s first task may be deciding what Starling wants to be when it grows up.

A spokesman for Starling Bank said: “The Starling Group is on track for a sixth straight year of profitability on strong customer growth and diversification. Starling Bank is tripling retail and SME account openings year-on-year as it attracts new customers to its innovative products and AI-powered in-app features, all backed by 24/7, UK-based human service.

“Engine by Starling is also scaling rapidly, having doubled its client count in the last financial year, with more announcements of long-term contracts to come.”

data.title: Britain can’t afford any more quangos
data.description:
Who says Andy Burnham doesn’t do anything of significance? In the last few days, his Government has created “water councils” to supervise an industry that is already collapsing under the weight of over-regulation, as well as a “special health authority” to absorb staff from NHS England.

At this rate, we are well on track for a hundred or more new regulatory, supervisory or advisory bodies a year, each one equipped with generously paid staff and swish London offices, plus the obligatory satellite branch in Bolton. 

This is crazy. The British economy can’t afford all the quangos – we should be abolishing them instead.

If you happen to have some spare time on your hands, and feel like a cushy gig, I recommend applying for one of the new water councils.

Apparently there will be eight of them across the country, designed, in the words of Burnham, to give local people “a real say over what they need from their water company”.

Never mind that we already have one water regulator, Ofwat, with an annual budget of £78m, as well as consultative bodies, such as Water Resources East, not to mention the whole series of financial regulators that all the regional water companies have to deal with.

It seems what we need is just one more layer of oversight.

Likewise, most of us might imagine that the answer to the question of “what do we need from our water company” would be pretty straightforward. Clean water, and enough of it that we can use the sprinklers in the garden over a hot summer, with fewer leaks, and lower bills. But, hey, whatever. It seems we don’t need more engineers, or reservoirs, or any of that stuff. We need a “council” where things can be “discussed”.

Similarly, some of us might have imagined that getting rid of NHS England would mean streamlining the health service. But no.

The Special Health Authority is designed to provide jobs for all the people who might otherwise lose them. It will probably be “special” for them, if not for patients.

Meanwhile, back in September, the Government announced the creation of the OneGov Delivery Agency, due for launch next spring, with a budget still to be determined, while Great British Railways has now been formally launched, with Sir John Kingman bringing all his commercial nous as a former permanent secretary to the Treasury to make trains “great” again.

It probably won’t be long before we see the launch of Great British Steel for all the nationalised metal-bashing assets.

The list goes on and on. It seems like a long time since Sir Keir Starmer – if anyone still remembers him – promised a “bonfire of the quangos”. Instead, the Government is launching new ones at an accelerating rate. There doesn’t seem to be any issue that ministers don’t think can be solved by a task force, a council or a special advisory committee.

The trouble is, none of them is actually going to make anything any better.

There are three big problems. To start with, the costs keep adding up. According to figures from the TaxPayer’s Alliance, 438 quangos received total funding of £378bn in the last full financial year.

Between them, they employ almost half a million people. True, some of that is money that the Government would have been spending anyway, except that it has been outsourced to a separate agency.

But each layer adds costs of its own. There are offices to be paid for, and consultants to be hired, and staff, complete with generous pensions, to be added to the payroll. Each one is, without question, more expensive than if the Government were simply doing the work directly.

Next, it means proliferating red tape. As soon as a new council or agency is created it has to keep itself busy. That only means one thing. It has to keep creating new regulations, and targets, followed by reports on their implementation, and fines for anyone who does not follow the rules.

Finally, all quangos expand. They have to build their empires, just like any organisation, and the only way they can do that is by taking on more people, and interfering even more with whatever industry they are meant to be looking after. We can see that very clearly in their budgets.

Why is Ofwat spending 9pc more this year than last year? It is hard to argue the water industry is 9pc better run.

Or why does the Office of Rail and Road need a 5.75pc budget increase, especially given that most of the rail industry has been taken back into state ownership, so it is hard to figure out why we even need it at all.

No quango in human history ever volunteered to close itself down, or for its funding to be reduced, and there is no chance that any Labour minister will ever demand that it does. Instead, they just expand relentlessly.

The British economy is turning into one giant regulatory body with a country attached.

It is crushing growth, stifling genuine entrepreneurship, and running up huge bills that the economy can barely afford. Even by the standards of this Labour Government, two new quangos in a single week is an alarming rate of increase. At best, they will absorb time and money, while making no positive difference to anything.

At worst, they will make each industry they meddle in even more hopelessly inefficient. The only solution is to sweep them all away – but unfortunately there is very little chance of that happening under this Government.

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: Elon Musk to kill off Tesla’s Cybertruck
data.description:
Elon Musk is to end production of Tesla’s Cybertruck after sales of the controversial electric pick-up proved a disappointment.

The electric carmaker’s chief executive signalled last night that production of the Cybertruck will wind down in 2027, making way for the business to produce more robotaxis at its Texas Gigafactory.

Posting on social media, Mr Musk said: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

The announcement comes just three years after the Cybertruck first went on sale.

Mr Musk had hailed the three-ton vehicle as “bulletproof” and “apocalypse-proof”, while the company’s website promotes its “ultra-hard stainless-steel exoskeleton” and a range of up to 325 miles.

However, the truck’s high price dampened demand among motorists.

It was initially set to cost $39,999 (£30,600) but the cheapest version now starts at $60,000 (£45,900).

Tesla sold just 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first nine months of 2026, according to analysts Cox Automotive, far below Mr Musk’s previous predictions of 250,000 sales a year.

While Mr Musk had billed the pick-up as the ultimate off-road electric vehicle, the Cybertruck has suffered from a series of mishaps and faults before and after it went on sale.

When demonstrating the truck’s toughened glass during its 2019 launch event, a Tesla executive threw a ball bearing at its window, causing it to shatter.

Tesla has also been forced to issue recalls of the truck over braking issues and other problems, including the vehicle’s trim falling off.

Several trucks have been involved in accidents where they have burst into fireballs after a crash.

Mr Musk took the decision to end production as he attempts to revive Tesla by focusing on AI, robotics and driverless taxis, increasing production of its Cybercab vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots.

The company has launched ride-hailing services in a handful of US cities, while it is planning to build up to 125,000 autonomous electric cabs per year at its flagship Texas plant.

Shares in Mr Musk’s companies have plunged this week after the Democrats swung to victory in the US midterm elections, taking both the House and the Senate.

Tesla’s stock is down more than 12pc since Tuesday, while SpaceX is down 11pc. Mr Musk’s net worth plummeted by close to $80bn in one day on Thursday to around $785bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

data.title: Britain’s energy policy is driving us to Middle East, says gas storage boss
data.description:
The owner of one of Britain’s biggest gas-storage facilities is ditching investment in the UK for the Middle East because of the Government’s crippling energy policies, its chief executive said.

Peter Mann, head of energy group Kistos, said future spending by the company would go to places such as Oman because the UK lacked a stable tax regime for oil and gas.

He said the Middle East would remain more appealing than the UK until energy strategy was taken out of ministers’ hands and given to an independent regulatory body.

Mann said this would mean “people know where they stand”.

“That ultimately is the key to investment. That stability has gone in the UK,” he said.

Kistos Energy owns Hill Top, one of the few remaining gas storage sites in the UK that can deliver the gas equivalent of 11pc of the UK’s daily total.

The 46-year-old, son of colourful ex-army officer and mercenary Simon Mann, and, like his father, a former officer in the Scots Guards, founded the company just six years ago.

Since then it has followed a trajectory similar, albeit on a smaller scale, to that of Neo Next+, the 2018 start-up that is now the UK North Sea’s biggest operator.

Both have bought up assets pioneered by energy majors but then sold off as they quit the North Sea – driven out by the UK’s divisive energy politics.

Mann says he would like to invest more in the UK, including in gas storage projects like Hill Top, but is exasperated by the constant regulatory changes politicians have imposed on the oil and gas industry in recent years.

Kistos is still investing in the UK – but only just.

It has bought the nearby Hole House gas caverns too and plans to reopen them for gas storage in the next couple of years.

Mann thinks Kistos is the only UK company spending private capital to actually increase the country’s domestic gas storage capacity.

Back in 2022, it also bought into gas production with stakes in four fields off the Shetlands known as the Greater Laggan area, along with associated pipelines and a gas plant.

But frustrated by an unpredictable windfall tax regime, bureaucratic paralysis over North Sea drilling and a political class that treats energy policy as a tactical football, Kistos’s future investments are mostly heading abroad.

It has recently spent $148m (£110m) on stakes in oil fields in Oman, with plans to invest a further $100m in the next three years, plus similar amounts in Norway’s North Sea – where Kistos bought Mime Petroleum in 2023.

“I think we are the only ones in the UK investing in increasing the capacity of gas storage at this point in time ... But Kistos is not in a place where it has to do things just in the UK, so we can be selective and opportunistic in where we see value,” he says.

Such views are increasingly common in the UK oil and gas sector.

For Britain, the consequences of this domestic investment freeze are severe – the decline of the North Sea and the UK’s inadequate storage means the country haemorrhages billions each year.

That goes on importing foreign energy – especially gas – subsidising overseas jobs and tax revenues while exposing British households to extreme winter volatility.

If Britain manages to keep the lights on and avoid gas shortages this coming winter, it will be thanks in no small part to some of the nation’s largest but least visible assets which are owned by Kistos.

They lie deep beneath the rolling fields of Cheshire comprising an array of giant salt caverns pumped full of pressurised natural gas which are now amongst our most vital gas supply bulwarks.

Cheshire’s salt caverns are among the UK’s least appreciated geological assets. Around 200 million years ago the region was covered in shallow seas that evaporated, leaving salt layers hundreds of metres thick, now buried deep underground.

They have been mined for centuries – providing, for example, the rock salt that keeps our roads free of ice.

But it’s the impermeable caverns drilled into the remaining salt, 600 metres below ground, that are now filled with gas, the region’s most vital energy asset.

“Our caverns are connected to the national transmission network,” said Mann. “We can empty them really quickly and do 11pc of [the] UK’s daily gas requirement, but then you can fill it up quite quickly in three or four days and do the same thing again.”

That facility means companies like Kistos can respond fast to changes in demand for gas – releasing more if temperatures plunge and demand surges. Or soaking up surpluses when demand falls.

That buffers the UK’s gas consumers against shortages. And it’s also profitable – for example by exploiting price swings to buy when demand falls or supply surges, and then reselling as prices go up.

It sounds like an easy way to make money, but Kistos is now one of just a handful of companies still operating in this market.

Its nearest rival is Storengy, a subsidiary of French energy giant Engie, which runs the nearby Stublach site.

Another used to be Centrica, owners of British Gas and of the much larger Rough gas storage site – a depleted gas field in the North Sea that could hold about three weeks’ worth of UK gas supply.

However, Chris O’Shea, the Centrica boss, has declared that the site cannot run at a profit and plans to shut it down next April – unless the Government provides funding.

The caverns under Cheshire that now help underpin UK gas supplies could have gone the same way.

Another facility at Hatfield Moor, near Doncaster, shut down two decades ago, while EDF shut down the Hole House site, in Cheshire, just a few years ago. Hole House is now being reopened by Kistos.

Those closures are one reason why the UK is facing this winter with a wafer-thin margin of gas reserves. “We now have just six or seven days of security of storage available in the UK,” warns Mann.

His warnings are echoed by many others.

UK storage is only 36pc full, according to energy economist Nick Butler, a former BP vice-president and Downing Street adviser.

“That is well below the level in other countries across Europe ... In the circumstances, it is surprising that the UK Energy Secretary has not made a statement on the issue to Parliament,” he wrote on Substack.

Until the UK restores commercial sanity to its energy policy, Cheshire’s salt caverns will remain an isolated buffer against the cold while British capital investment continues to find a warmer, more welcoming home under the desert sun.

data.title: The 33-year-old at the forefront of Britain’s defence revolution
data.description:
To see the future of Britain’s defence industry, you have to visit a four-storey building found on what used to be a car park off Old Kent Road. This clean and functional edifice is the biggest new factory in London since the Second World War.

A Union Flag overlooks the factory floor, where 12 machines are silently engaged in turning steel, aluminium and titanium into precision components for jet engines, drones, robots and much more.

Presiding over them is Alexander Fitzgerald, the 33-year-old founder and chief executive of the company, Isembard, which he established in late 2024.

Like everyone who creates a successful business, the T-shirt-wearing entrepreneur spotted a problem and proposed a solution. “What’s happening across every single sector right now – from aerospace to defence to robotics to energy to semiconductors – is that demand is massively increasing, but the supply of manufacturing capacity to make those components is reducing,” he says.

Isembard’s driving purpose is to provide some of that desperately needed extra capacity. The opportunity is all the greater because of a revolution sweeping Britain’s defence industry.

For generations, the sector has been dominated by a handful of large “prime contractors”, such as BAE Systems, which specialise in the slow and hugely expensive production of a relative handful of advanced jet fighters, tanks and warships, designed to stay in service for decades.

But the lesson from Ukraine is that there are increasing – and critical – advantages for countries that can speedily produce an abundance of smaller and cheaper systems, such as drones, then constantly improve and redesign them, and turn out new and better models every few months. This requires a multitude of small and medium-sized enterprises that can compete to be the most innovative and efficient by deploying AI to make an ever-changing array of components as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Isembard is already doing exactly that. Companies send 3D designs for the parts they need, and Isembard manufactures them according to those designs. “We build our own software and AI to make setting up our factories and running our factories really efficient,” says Fitzgerald.

At present, about 95 per cent of components for manufacturing are produced by small and medium-scale businesses. It is an extraordinary fact that the average age of the owners of these companies in the UK is 65 – and that no less than 40 per cent of them plan to retire within five years.

At the exact moment when Europe is rearming – with all Nato countries, including Britain, pledging to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 – the supply chain for new components is contracting.

Hence, Isembard is expanding rapidly to meet pent-up demand. Fitzgerald opened his first factory last year, and today his company has 18 worldwide – eight in Britain, eight in America and one each in France and Germany.

This growth has been accelerated by Isembard’s unique business model, which allows for franchised factories. All but five of the existing plants are not owned by the company, but franchised to individual operators. The newest, in Swindon, took a mere 90 days to set up, and Fitzgerald aims to get this down to one or two weeks.

Speed and agility are everything. Fitzgerald notes that what has allowed Ukraine to resist the Russian invaders is not one kind of exquisitely engineered drone, but rather a vast and constantly changing array of different models. “In Ukraine, it’s not one type of drone – and 10 billion of them,” he says. “It’s a zoo of different types of drones, at all classes and all stages. Then you need to be able to scale up.”

Fitzgerald adds: “You need a manufacturing base, which is fundamentally a question of, ‘Have you got enough stuff that can make stuff? Have you networked them enough to be more efficient?’ That’s really the core of our business.”

Reindustrialising Britain by reshoring production is, he believes, the key to the country’s future prosperity. “The grand theory of everything is manufacturing because it’s the root of our prosperity, security and purpose,” he says. “I subscribe to the manufacturing dream – that means security and prosperity [depend on] your ability to make stuff.”

Nearby, the computer numerical control (CNC) machines – which have affectionate nicknames such as Cathy and Big Bertha – on the factory floor are playing their part in reindustrialising Britain by turning out the precisely shaped objects that will soon be flying at high speed as the components of jet engines or drones.

The factory, which covers three floors and 160,000 square feet, aims to triple its workforce to 200 by the end of next year. Taking delivery of the hulking CNCs required Fitzgerald to install a bigger loading door in the building, which was previously used as a grocery depot. The machines had to arrive in the early hours of the morning, since there are timing restrictions within three miles of Charing Cross for loads of that weight and size.

Fitzgerald emphasises that Isembard is not a “defence tech company”, but rather a “manufacturing company”. About 60 per cent of its customers are in aerospace and defence, while most of the rest are in robotics.

But Russia is unlikely to be interested in that distinction as its intelligence services carry out their escalating campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe, including in Britain.

Is Fitzgerald concerned about that threat? “Yes, and I think the Government should be concerned,” he replies. “We have good security protections in both the cyber and the physical side. We’ve had a lot of support from the Government, and from the police and other agencies, as well.”

Fitzgerald has personal experience of Whitehall, since he spent three years as a Treasury civil servant after graduating from Nottingham University with a degree in biochemistry. Earlier, he had also tried his hand at journalism as an intern at City AM.

He enjoyed his time working in the Government, but cannot help remembering: “When I thought I had the right answer for something, it still had to go through six pairs of hands to get to someone to make a decision. That frustrated me.”

He left the Treasury to start a broadband company that amassed almost 100,000 customers before he sold it to Octopus Group in 2022. Fitzgerald founded Isembard soon afterwards, and the company now makes components for customers like Anduril, which manufactures drones and autonomous weaponry, and Oxford Space Systems, which produces the antennae for satellites.

In the past, certain British investors and banks had a fastidious disdain for any businesses linked to defence, some of which were denied financial services. Fitzgerald, who is also an Army reservist, has encountered no such difficulties, and he believes that attitudes have changed. “I think Ukraine has changed that,” he says. “Geopolitics has changed that.”

Something else that has changed is the attitude towards manufacturing in general. One of Andy Burnham’s central priorities is “reindustrialisation” and recapturing the dynamism of former years.

In that spirit, Fitzgerald named his company after the great Victorian engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, though he adapted the spelling of his hero’s Christian name because the original domain had already been taken.

Today, he keeps a black top hat on his desk in tribute to the man whose individual drive and genius powered Britain’s first industrial revolution.

His other inspiration is Lord Beaverbrook, the minister for aircraft production in 1940, who galvanised British industry into delivering 100 Spitfires and Hurricanes every week, making him an architect of victory in the Battle of Britain and changing the course of the Second World War.

“The Air Ministry didn’t like him. He was threatening to resign the whole time, but he got the job done,” says Fitzgerald, who notes that Beaverbrook tripled production in a matter of months by distributing the manufacture of Spitfire and Hurricane components between hundreds of superbly innovative and cost-efficient small and medium enterprises across the country.

That formula saved Britain in 1940. It might yet do the same again.

data.title: Workers fear losing jobs over train delays, warn MPs
data.description:
Workers fear losing their jobs because rail services are regularly late, MPs have warned.

A spate of line closures and cancellations during the summer heatwaves made it impossible for thousands of commuters to arrive at the office on time.

MPs at a Westminster Hall debate said workers were increasingly fearful of the lack of reliable train connections and urged the Government to spend more on rail infrastructure to improve punctuality.

Charlotte Cane, the Liberal Democrat MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, said: “One [constituent] in particular has written to say that because their train has been so unreliable for getting to their job in London that their employer is now putting them under pressure.

“They are becoming an unreliable member of staff and their employer doesn’t know when they are going to turn up to work.

“They are also having to make up the time at the end of the day, which means they are getting home very late. It makes it a complete nightmare for them.”

Desperate to protect their jobs, some workers were now considering moving house to be closer to stations with more reliable services, MPs said.

Others are considering giving up well-paid positions in London and other major cities for less lucrative roles closer to home.

Among the worst-hit lines this summer was the route between King’s Cross and King’s Lynn via Cambridge and Ely, the later of which lies in Ms Cane’s constituency.

It suffered three months of disruption, including 900 cancellations after normally damp peat beneath the tracks dried out, leading the ground to become uneven.

James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, which includes King’s Lynn, said people from the town who worked in Cambridge and London had found the disruption intolerable.

He told The Telegraph: “I’ve had quite a number of constituents who have said they’re thinking of moving jobs. They’ve been in tears and incredibly stressed.

“One lady said her husband, who commutes and is self-employed, had been driven to depression and was having suicidal thoughts because he was worried that he wouldn’t be able to provide for his family. It’s pushing people to breaking point.”

Mr Wild said some commuters had opted to drive to Peterborough on the East Coast Main Line, or Norwich, which has trains to Liverpool Street – both an hour away by road – to be sure of getting to work.

He said there were concerns that with the line suffering heat-related disruption for the past two summers, people would stop viewing King’s Lynn as a viable commuter town, which could have a knock-on effect on house prices.

Mr Wild questioned Andy Burnham about the matter in September, when the Prime Minister said he would “convene a rail summit soon”.

Richard Foord, the Liberal Democrat MP for Honiton and Sidmouth, said commuters to cities beyond London had also been affected.

He said restrictions imposed between London Waterloo and the West Country had in one case led a dental hygienist to cancel her 9am appointments “indefinitely”.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for local transport, said he could not rule out further weather-related disruption.

He added that while speed restrictions and closures might be frustrating, the railway’s primary duty was to keep passengers safe.

data.title: Six tips for a smooth home renovation, from a luxury interior designer
data.description:
Bee Janaye is an interior designer on a mission to demystify the renovation process for homeowners. In addition to working on high-end projects across London and as far as Canada with her design studio, By Janaye, she is also prolific on TikTok and Instagram, where she shares tips, advice, and occasionally – controversial opinions (under the handle @diaryofahomedesigner).

“There is a lack of transparency about how much time and how many decisions are actually required to build the dream home that people see on Pinterest,” notes Janaye of the industry. She believes that soaring costs for labour and building materials have made doing up a property “a lifestyle choice”, and that trying to emulate the style of picture-perfect rooms on social media has led to a state of overwhelm for those outside the profession.

“Interior designers spend months designing every detail of a space before they go to build. It’s a full-time job, and one we’ve spent years learning from,” says Janaye, squashing the misconception that designers are simply drafted in to choose cushions and what to hang on the walls. Janaye would encourage anyone embarking on a gut renovation without the means for a designer to mastermind the look and feel of each room in the same way a professional would. “Everyone needs a collection of images or samples for each phase. They need to plan, plan, plan, and work to a set budget. If self-managing the build, consider taking time off work to do so,” she says.

In her own words, Janaye shares the professional tips she uses with her high-end clients to help make every project run smoothly and gives consistent results.

Design for how you live — then choose the finishes (not the other way around)

I encourage people to spend time really considering what it is they love about their current spaces, what drives them crazy, and what they would like to change. They write this down and these become anchors, long before we start discussing finishes.

A renovator needs to be able to articulate why something works best for them, for example choosing an integrated oven at eye level because they have had a bad back, or their need for a larger dining table. This creates a good position to make solid choices from. A key mistake I see people jumping the gun with is choosing a style of flooring very early on – such as chevron or herringbone – but by the time they’ve worked out all the other finishes, they realise it’s all going to look too busy. It’s the same with wall paint colours: you need to pick the furniture first.

Don’t let tradespeople dictate your lighting scheme

I don’t believe that you can have a well-designed space without beautiful lighting. An electrician is an expert in wiring and circuits, but not the one to warn you that a dozen spotlights in the ceiling is going to make a room feel sterile. Anyone can make their own lighting plan using a basic layout (or estate agent’s floor plan) of their home. Add in furniture placement and draw in what you think you need: such as a pendant over a dining table; wall lights around a banquette seat.

If you are planning for a reading corner in your lounge with a big cosy chair, why not put in an off-centre pendant to make a feature of it? This all needs to be planned long before the electrician is on site. Otherwise the builder will cost for a set amount of power points and when you start adding a picture light here and a pendant there, it won’t fall within the budget and costs start spiralling.

Get your builder to give itemised quotes

You can’t whittle down a builder from vague, blanket numbers. We compile a line-by-line itemisation of the work required in each space, which is known as a tender pack. This enables building firms to quote for a project accurately and crucially, it means we can compare estimates on a like-for-like basis.

Any homeowner can do this using a mock-up document online (do be warned: it is a time-intensive process). If this isn’t done, then there is no point obtaining several quotes because they won’t be comparable. A builder estimating tens of thousands less than another without understanding what the renovation costs are for means nothing, because you have no idea what you are comparing. It breaks my heart when clients simply opt for the cheapest and subsequently rack-up dozens of “extras”.

Spend your renovation budget in the right order

No-one should be shopping for their sofa before they’ve locked in their build budget. Homeowners need to understand what the first fix will cost, which will get the property to a reasonable shell. After that it’s fixed finishes: tiles, flooring, sanitaryware; these have to be prioritised. On second fix a space should be liveable. Only then do furniture and soft furnishings come in.

I’m of the view that these can be phased; if you have to wait a little bit longer to buy the curtains that you really want, then it’s worth it. Approach the project the other way around and you’ll definitely spend a lot more than you planned to.

Have a clear purpose when it comes to fitted joinery

Joinery is so expensive now; I’d rather clients had temporary pieces such as free-standing shelves or rails for wardrobes while they figure out what storage they actually need in that space. I used to work for a high-street fitted-furniture company and the designers work on commission, so while someone might think they’re getting a free design service, the real goal is to sell.

Often people will rush into having wardrobes fitted without really considering what they need to store: standard shelves and rails aren’t always the best option. The same applies to living room joinery: just because everyone else has shelves either side of a chimney breast, it doesn’t mean you have to do the same.

Don’t default to fitting the sink on a kitchen island

We design homes for our clients around their lifestyle, so if someone doesn’t stack the dishwasher immediately, then a pile of dirty dishes in plain sight perhaps isn’t the best option for an open-plan kitchen. People often think that a hob is a messier island option than a sink, but a sleek induction hob is much more aesthetically pleasing than a sink.

What it comes down to is really considering how you’re going to use a space and make decisions accordingly, rather than opting for what everyone else is doing. There’s a fear around making choices that are different, which is why I started sharing advice on social media. Think outside the box and do something because you genuinely like it.

data.title: Swiss face £9bn bill to keep trains running on time
data.description:
Switzerland’s trains are celebrated for their immaculate punctuality. But now the country is facing a £9bn bill to stop its rail services becoming like those in Germany, its erratic neighbour.

The country’s largest railway operator, state-owned SBB, has said its backlog of repairs to tracks and signal boxes rose 12pc last year to 9.5bn Swiss francs (£8.6bn).

If the repairs aren’t carried out, SBB has warned that Switzerland risks “a situation similar to that in other countries” – a reference to Germany, where the formerly clockwork-like train network has become notoriously unreliable.

So far, the Swiss trains are holding the line on their fabled punctuality. This year 94pc of its trains have arrived within three minutes of their scheduled time, about the same rate as the previous two years.

No other major European country gets above 90pc, and many have resorted to using a looser definition of punctuality.

Britain scored 84pc last year. Germany clocked 88pc, but that excludes cancelled trains and defines punctual as within six minutes. Even on that metric, just 60pc of Germany’s long-distance and high-speed trains run on time.

Germany’s decline arose from underinvestment in maintenance. As it tries to play catch-up, large sections of track often have to be closed for repairs, making punctuality even worse.

Switzerland will be keen to avoid that fate.

But SBB is at loggerheads with the Swiss government, which instead wants to spend 20bn Swiss francs (CHF).on expanding and embellishing the rail network.

This could include building a whole new station at Lucerne, at a potential cost of more than CHF 3bn, and a 17-mile tunnel with a potential budget of CHF 800m.

SBB, in a submission to a public consultation, urged the authorities to prioritise fixing the existing network over any major expansion.

Both sides agree, though, that the signalling system also needs a technological overhaul that will cost a further CHF 9bn.

This week SBB kicked off the first CHF 2bn tender for the IT revamp. The full digitalisation of signalling will cost another CHF 7bn by 2045, but so far the government has budgeted just CHF 1bn for this process.

Meanwhile, money is tight for the essential repairs to keep the trains running on time. SBB has said it needs to repair at least 143 miles of track a year, but last year only managed 116 miles.

Funding for its track and signalling work comes from a separate Rail Infrastructure Fund, which is bankrolled by annual contributions from the national and cantonal governments, alongside some hypothecated portions of VAT, income tax and the mineral oil tax. Some of this funding is due to expire in 2030.

data.title: Thousands of households to receive Amazon deliveries by drone
data.description:
Thousands of households across the UK will start receiving Amazon deliveries by drone after the tech giant expanded its use of the technology.

Amazon launched a trial of its Prime Air service in May that enabled parcels weighing up to 2.2kg to be delivered to around 600 households within a 7.5-mile radius of its Darlington warehouse.

The company is now extending this service to around 8,000 households after securing a key approval from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).

Prime Air allows customers to order a range of small products, including baby formula, household essentials and tech supplies, for delivery in under two hours at no additional cost.

Packages no bigger than a shoebox are carried by Amazon’s MK30 drone, which features six propeller blades, and dropped from around 12ft into customers’ gardens.

Amazon expanded the service after becoming the first drone operator in the world to secure authorisation and flight-worthiness validation from the CAA.

The regulator reviewed the safety features of Amazon’s electric drones, which use machine learning to monitor surrounding airspace and steer.

As they descend, the drones use these systems to detect obstacles that would not appear on a satellite map, such as clotheslines or trampolines.

Theunis Scheepers, the director of Prime Air Europe, said: “For customers in Darlington it means getting what they need quickly, safely, and reliably, and it is the foundation for bringing Prime Air to more of the UK.”

Amazon has been bogged down in a lengthy struggle to launch drone deliveries, with its efforts hindered by technical challenges and red tape.

Jeff Bezos first pledged to introduce drone deliveries in the UK 13 years ago. The company made a handful of deliveries to rural areas around Cambridge in 2016, but the service never developed beyond a small trial.

Amazon was previously hoping to deploy the service in 2024, but that deadline has repeatedly been pushed back amid negotiations with the CAA.

The company has been offering drone deliveries in some US cities since 2022, where delivery times are just 36 minutes.

Sophie O’Sullivan, at the CAA, said: “This first in-kind announcement marks another important step towards safely integrating new technologies into UK airspace, supporting growth, and helping to ensure the UK remains a world leader in aerospace innovation.

“It also reflects the wider progress being made as the aviation sector evolves and new technologies become part of everyday operations.”

data.title: Trump rages at Fox News as Republican voters switch off
data.description:
As the results began to flood in on a bruising midterm election night for the Republicans, Donald Trump picked an unlikely scapegoat: Fox News.

The US president, evidently glued to Fox’s coverage, took aim at the channel’s polls and choice of guests in a slew of angry late-night posts on Truth Social.

“FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” he wrote.

At the same time, he hit the network with a dig about its viewership. “FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me – My numbers are better than they have ever been.”

The comments came even as Trump called and texted into the Murdoch-owned news network, which has long been his biggest cheerleader and helped bring him to power. It underscores the complex, co-dependent relationship between the two.

The Democrats’ stunning midterms victory raises questions about Fox’s place in the media landscape, amid a sharp drop in ratings. Once an all-powerful force in US politics, its influence is fading.

A lame-duck Trump is ostensibly more bad news for the network. For all the talk of balance, no individual has come to embody Fox more than Trump. His bolshy and erratic behaviour has dominated the news agenda and provided news fodder for more than a third of the network’s life.

A spurred and vengeful Trump may present more fodder for the network, as will coverage of the wave of “far-Left” Democrats who have now come to power. But there is no guarantee that audiences will stick with them for these stories. Many have already jumped ship to YouTube or streamers.

For cable news networks, election nights are often compared to the Super Bowl as droves of viewers tune in for blow-by-blow updates. Fox even deployed a special chatbot providing real-time answers to audience questions.

The run-up to the midterms provided ample material, with Trump facing off against Barack Obama on the campaign trail in recent weeks.

Yet Fox’s ratings have been anything but blockbuster. Fox News attracted an average audience of 1.1 million in October, down 27pc compared to last year, according to official figures from Nielsen.

In primetime hours between 8pm and 11pm, Fox pulled in fewer than 1.7 million viewers, down from 2.3 million at the same time last year. The network looks set to record its worst-performing month for overall viewers since December 2023.

The decline has not escaped the attention of Fox bosses. Lachlan Murdoch, the 55-year-old scion whose ascension to the throne of the family empire was confirmed last year following a fraught succession battle, this week admitted that the network had been hit by “viewer fatigue”.

“It was a tremendous news cycle this time last year, which we’re comping against,” he told investors, pointing to events in 2025, including the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Murdoch insisted that this was a broader trend, rather than a reflection on Fox specifically.

“Those viewers are not going to any other news channel,” he said. “They’re not switching to MS Now or to CNN. They’re just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.”

Yet these claims are undermined by viewing figures for both CNN and MS Now – the network formerly known as MSNBC – which grew 19pc and 13pc in primetime respectively last month.

“Human nature is at play here, especially when it comes to political news consumption where people seek affirmation that ‘their side’ is right and winning when momentum is in their favour,” says Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester.

“When that’s not the case, people can shut down and seek an escape from reality, which results in news avoidance.”

Fox remains the largest cable news network. The company argues that its rivals are growing from a low comparison last year and say the network enjoyed its highest-rating midterm year ever despite the slump.

A spokesman said: “Fox News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter century, throughout every administration since 2001.

“More recently, the network has expanded its dominance beyond linear, where it is not only the top-rated cable network on television, but dominates digital, streaming, social media and YouTube, generating nearly four billion YouTube video views this year alone.”

Nevertheless, the weakness during what should be a strong period for viewing figures points at a tougher future ahead.

Cable networks have for years been battling an exodus of audiences to streaming alternatives, known in the US as “cord-cutting”. Fox last year launched its own streaming service – Fox One – in an effort to counteract this trend.

Proulx says traditional TV has “lost its grip on non-boomer audiences”. A recent survey showed that while 44pc of US baby boomers said traditional TV takes up most of their weekly entertainment time, that figure tumbles to 19pc of Gen X, 5pc of millennials and only 3pc of Gen Z.

For Fox, these industry trends are exacerbated by its complex entanglement with Trump, an avid viewer of the channel.

Two prominent figures in the Trump administration – Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, and Jeanine Pirro, the United States attorney for the District of Columbia – are former Fox hosts. Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former White House press secretary, has joined Fox as a pundit and defended the president on election night.

In turn, the US president has been a rich source of material.

Trump’s 2016 election victory delivered a record audience, which was beaten only by the 14.1 million people who tuned in during the 2020 vote, when Murdoch’s network infuriated the president with an early call for Joe Biden in Arizona.

Other events, including Trump’s impeachment and attempted assassination, have also delivered major spikes in the channel’s audience, in a phenomenon described as the “Trump bump”.

“My view would be, based upon a decade of Trump as president with the Biden interregnum, that he is fantastic for news media,” says analyst Alex DeGroote. “He sets the news agenda every day, whether you like him or hate him.”

This has been handsomely profitable for Fox, which reported $350m (£260m) in political advertising revenue in its latest quarter, representing a record for the midterm period.

But Trump has blown hot and cold with his long-time ally Rupert Murdoch. A US judge last week dismissed Trump’s $10bn lawsuit against Murdoch’s Wall Street Journal over its reporting of a letter the president allegedly wrote to Jeffrey Epstein.

Fox was forced to cough up nearly $800m in 2023 to settle a defamation lawsuit over its reporting of Trump’s stolen election claims, showing the cost of unwavering support for the president.

With Trump now a lame duck, Fox’s ratings slump may worsen.

“I think the key question is: is this the beginning of a downward trend?” says DeGroote.

“He’s magnetic viewing, but we are closer to the end than the beginning, and it may well be that the second half of his presidency is less box-office than the first half.”

Conversely, if an angered Trump employs a scorched-earth policy it would create ever more headlines.

“I think you could make a case that we could be in for a real period of friction, which could lead to even more electric viewing and even more outlandish episodes,” says DeGroote.

The renewed power of the Democrats could also provide compulsive “hate-watching” for Fox’s core audience.

The network has repeatedly referred to Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat firebrand who has become the first Muslim US senator after his victory in Michigan, as “far-Left”.

More broadly, its coverage has painted a picture of a socialist takeover of the US Left, with stories highlighting divisions within the Democratic Party over progressive policies such as abolishing ICE and the proposed Medicare for All.

Tom Emmer, the Republican House majority whip, summed up the position during an appearance on Fox Business’s The Bottom Line, saying: “There’s nothing democratic about socialism.”

Yet Republicans may watch these dramas play out elsewhere. Some of the network’s most outspoken former stars, including Tucker Carlson and Megyn Kelly, have pursued their own shows on YouTube. Trump, who can reach his supporters directly via Truth Social, recently also launched his own channel on the streaming platform.

At the same time, Fox’s arch-rival on the other side of the political spectrum, CNN, is bracing for its own shake-up under the ownership of David Ellison, a Trump ally.

Industry watchers believe he could try to shift the editorial line of CNN. Ellison, who took control of the network following a $100bn merger between Paramount and Warner Bros, has already proven controversial for his editorial interference in CBS News.

Despite a calamitous night, Trump is not done yet. Nevertheless, with the end of his administration now in sight, bosses know the curtain will soon be coming down on the Trump show. It is a problem that Fox News executives must figures out how to confront.

“We’ll look back on this time in a few years and think it was the most extraordinary period ever,” says DeGroote.

“It will be very quiet and boring when Trump’s gone.”

data.title: The Walliams case shows why the rich must not be allowed to muzzle the press
data.description:
In the US, the counterproductive result of seeking an injunction is called “the Streisand effect”. In Britain, the effect is usually related to the massive sales of Spycatcher after Margaret Thatcher’s futile attempt to impose a worldwide ban on the book.

As David Walliams must recognise, if he glumly contemplates Wednesday’s newspapers and the many pages they devote to his obnoxious behaviour, any attempt to injunct the media gives the story more publicity than it would otherwise have received.

Barbra Streisand tried to injunct scientific photos of coastal erosion at her edge-of-cliff mansion in Malibu – only four had been downloaded before she brought the action but hundreds of thousands were after it failed. Spycatcher, a badly written conspiracy theory, sold more than a million copies worldwide on the strength of the government’s ill-conceived legal proceedings.

A threat to take your own life can never translate into a right to interfere with press freedom. But the very fact that Walliams’ lawyers thought this arguable draws attention to how English privacy law has developed to threaten freedom of speech.

Britain, to its discredit, had no protection for privacy until it adopted the European Convention on Human Rights in 1998. The right to “respect” for family life, home and correspondence stopped some press malpractice and served to close the News of the World, but it also provided a basis for oligarchs, tax evaders and wife-beaters to obtain injunctions against the release of information about which they could claim “a reasonable expectation of privacy”.

Judges in our highest court decided that this was an enormously wide field, not only covering physical and mental health but “racial or ethnic characteristics… the generality of personal and family relationships. Information conveyed in the course of personal relationships, a person’s political opinions and affiliations, religious commitments, personal financial and tax related information, past involvement in criminal behaviour…” and so on. Almost anything that a person can find embarrassing can be the subject of a claim for injunction, if the claimant can afford the legal costs (at least £50,000) of an application.

But the real danger in the explosion of privacy law is how it can chill public-interest reporting, especially in coverage of official abuse of power. In the Sir Cliff Richard case, for example, the police, without credible evidence, obtained and executed a search warrant and were obliged – rightfully so – to pay the pop star heavy damages. But he additionally won hundreds of thousands of pounds (and reportedly £1m in costs) from the BBC for televising the raid on his home.

The raid was the result of a warrant that should never have been granted, but the High Court ruled that all police suspects had “a reasonable expectation of privacy” at any stage of the investigation. This seriously handicaps the “watchdog” function of the media which cannot safely report on police dealings, however abusive, with named suspects. It allows the rich to threaten expensive actions against media who wish to expose their questionable commercial or tax dealings and personal affairs no matter how publicly important.

Injunctions are court orders not to publish the information set out in their schedules, on pain of up to two years’ imprisonment. MPs and peers are exempt when they speak under parliamentary privilege – as Lord Hain did when revealing that Sir Philip Green had obtained an injunction to stop The Daily Telegraph reporting allegations that he had sexually harassed and racially abused his staff. Such claims were not regarded by judges in 2018 as of sufficient public interest to override his privacy. But it is to be hoped that their attitudes have now changed.

There is no public list of injunctions that have been granted, and indeed there cannot be for “super injunctions” – the very mention of which is prohibited. In most cases the court will deliver a short public judgment setting out the law and the result and a long secret judgment assessing the facts. What happens to all these secret judgments? Where are they stored and how long must they stay secret? This is unclear.

For a nation that boasts of its “open justice” principle, it is entirely unsatisfactory. As Jeremy Bentham famously said “publicity is the very soul of justice” and courts should not keep secrets. We should at least appoint an “open-justice commissioner” to study and report on injunctions which impact upon public-interest reporting and act as custodian of the secret judgments handed down by our judges and direct their release when appropriate.

As for the damage done to individuals by exposing their private misbehaviour, the media must decide according to its own ethical standards and submit to public judgment. The Guardian was overkind to David Walliams, delaying publication for six months to allow him to make his hopeless case. His publishers, however, threatened to withdraw his popular children’s books, which seems an unnecessary act of censorship (should we really ban Alice in Wonderland because of Lewis Carroll’s alleged proclivities?).

The message of Walliams is clear: injunctions must not be allowed to suppress public interest reporting. And that there is a public interest in allowing women who claim to have been abused by powerful men to tell their stories if they are prepared to attest to the truth. Judges must drop their simplistic distinction between what merely interests the public (in which they find no value) and what is genuinely in the public interest by acknowledging that in the case of victims who want to speak out about sex abuse, it can be both.

Geoffrey Robertson KC founded Doughty Street Chambers and is the author of ‘Lawfare’ and (with Sir Andrew Nichol)‘Media Law’

data.title: Mike Ashley cements grip on Hugo Boss after chief executive resigns
data.description:
Mike Ashley has cemented his control over Hugo Boss following the appointment of a Frasers Group executive as the German retailer’s new chief.

David Epstein, the chief brand partnerships officer at Frasers, was confirmed as Hugo Boss’s new chief executive on Thursday following the resignation of Daniel Grieder.

He will take charge of the business on Jan 1.

Mr Epstein will join Michael Murray, Frasers’ chief executive, on the supervisory board of Hugo Boss after he was appointed chairman in September.

Mr Murray, who is also Mr Ashley’s son-in-law, is still in charge of Frasers, which owns Sports Direct, House of Fraser and luxury retailer Flannels.

Mr Ashley, who owns 74pc of Frasers, had previously ruled out installing Mr Murray as Hugo Boss’s chief executive but vowed to show the business a bit of “Dunkirk spirit”.

It comes after Frasers secured majority control of the business in October by raising its stake above 50pc, months after an unsuccessful €2bn (£1.67bn) takeover bid.

The pursuit forms part of an attempt by the British retailer, formerly known as Sports Direct, to expand upmarket into luxury and premium retail.

As well as building a stake in Hugo Boss, Frasers has also taken significant positions in Burberry and Mulberry. It also recently bought Harvey Nichols out of administration in a £40m deal.

Mr Epstein will take charge of Hugo Boss after managing brand partnerships across Frasers’ sport, premium, and luxury divisions since 2024.

Following his departure after five years at the helm, Mr Grieder said: “With this strong foundation in place, I am convinced that now is the right time for me to step down and hand over to the next generation of leadership.

“It has been an honour to lead Hugo Boss, and I will always feel connected to its people and brands.

Frasers began building its stake in Hugo Boss in 2020 and became its largest shareholder earlier this year after its takeover bid was rejected by the company’s board.

Mr Ashley has a history of taking minority stakes in retailers before seeking greater influence over their operations.

Frasers has also built positions in Asos and Boohoo,

However, its investments have not always paid off. Frasers bought luxury retailer Matches in late 2023 but placed it into administration less than three months later.

data.title: Octopus inheritance tax investors face £40m bill despite vow to waive fees
data.description:
Thousands of investors in Octopus’s inheritance tax scheme face £40m bill despite a pledge to waive some of its fees after its poor performance.

The investment firm last month pledged to scrap a lucrative annual management charge (AMC) it levied investors who had ploughed cash into the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS).

Erin Platts, the chief executive of Octopus Investments, said at the time it was about “drawing a line under” recent poor performance after the fund was forced to split in two.

However, an analysis of the fund’s performance suggests that while very few customers are liable to pay the AMC, investors will still face a £40m bill from a separate service fee charged on the scheme.

OITS has 18,000 customers and allows investors to lower their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses that qualify for relief.

Its customers were sold shares in Fern Trading, which owns about 300 energy, property and telecoms companies.

However, the fund was frozen to redemptions for nearly three months during the summer and was eventually split into two funds in October: Fern A, which has reopened to redemptions, and Fern B, which remains closed.

Octopus will still impose a 1.85pc service fee on the value of the Fern A fund, which is expected to bring in around £40m for Octopus Investments.

The levy on Fern B has been deferred and will apply only if the fund meets a certain return benchmark.

Alongside the service charges, Octopus also takes other fees, including the AMC, which is levied only when the fund returns more than 3pc a year.

A Telegraph analysis of Fern Trading’s share price record found that no group of investors who had invested in the scheme since 2011 reached the 3pc-a-year threshold.

Those who invested in 2011 have fared best, with annualised growth of about 2.2pc.

But returns have been negative for anyone who invested from 2022 onwards.

However, new investors could benefit from the waived fee.

Since Fern was founded in 2010, Octopus has collected more than £900m in fees from the trading business.

A spokesman for Octopus Investments said the firm had made significant changes to their fees.

“We’ve been clear that investment performance has been disappointing, and we’ve taken clear action to address those challenges and ensure we’ve best aligned our interests with customer outcomes,” they said.

“If we don’t deliver that outcome for customers, we don’t get the fee.”

data.title: Big banks ‘short-changing’ savers by failing to pass on rate rise
data.description:
Britain’s biggest banks have been accused of “short-changing” savers after failing to pass on higher interest rates to all of their customers.

The Bank of England raised its base rate by 0.25pc to 4pc on Nov 5 – the first increase in more than three years.

But the average easy-access savings account rate is now 2.61pc, just 0.03pc higher than last week, according to Moneyfacts.

The comparison website’s analysis showed that of the 28 savings providers which had increased rates so far, 70pc had at least one account where customers had received less than the full quarter-point rise. 

More than 100 providers have yet to make a decision on whether to raise rates.

HSBC raised its flexible saver account by just 0.05pc in response to the Bank’s decision this week. Nationwide is set to raise rates on most of its savings accounts by the full quarter-point on Dec 1, but customers with a Flex Instant Saver account will only see a 0.2pc rise.

Among Britain’s biggest banks – including Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, Nationwide, NatWest and Santander – the average return on their most flexible savings account stands at just 1.17pc.

Telegraph analysis on Friday showed that Tembo Money offered the top easy-access savings account with a rate of 5.5pc.

While many savers will not benefit immediately or in full from higher interest rates, homeowners on variable mortgages have seen their rates rise over the last eight days, with the average two-year rate increasing from 4.67pc to 4.89pc.

At the same time, the average two-year fixed-rate deal stands at 5.94pc, up from 4.83pc at the start of the year. This is because swap rates – benchmarks of future interest rates used by lenders to determine mortgage deals – had already priced in successive increases to the Bank rate.

Rachel Springall, of Moneyfacts, said: “Savers have so far been left short-changed following last week’s increase to the Bank of England base rate.

“The top rate deals remain on offer from challenger banks and building societies, so now is an ideal time to switch and ditch an old account to escape the ‘loyalty tax’ from their bank.”

Martyn James, a consumer rights expert, said: “We know from the speed with which mortgage rates get moved around at the merest hint of interest rate changes that financial services firms can be reactive. So why is it the complete opposite when it comes to savings?”

Ian Futcher, of wealth manager Quilter, said: “Some of this is because these providers know that many customers will simply leave their money where it is, even if they’re getting a poor deal. That inertia can prove very profitable, but it leaves loyal savers paying the price.”

After raising rates this week, the Bank of England blamed the ongoing conflict in the Middle East for triggering another sharp jump in energy prices.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said growing price pressures from the prolonged war in Iran meant the 0.25pc increase was “unlikely to be the last”.

Policymakers believe inflation will peak at around 5pc by the middle of 2027, even if the economy slows sharply.

HSBC and Nationwide were approached for comment.
