data.title: Nvidia approaches boss of Britain’s biggest tech firm to replace Huang
data.description:
The boss of British technology giant Arm has been approached about the possibility of leading Nvidia after Jensen Huang was ousted following a string of extramarital affairs.

Rene Haas, who has been at the helm of Cambridge-based Arm since 2022, is reportedly on a list of contenders to become Nvidia’s new chief executive.

Mr Haas previously held senior positions at Nvidia between 2006 and 2013, including running the company’s computing division.

He left to join Arm in 2013, rising to become chief executive before the company listed on the New York stock market in 2023.

Alongside running Arm, Mr Haas, who is based in California, serves as chief executive of SoftBank’s international division, helping to oversee the Japanese investment giant’s overseas subsidiaries.

Arm is best known for designing critical chip technology used on mobile phones, but has increasingly shifted to developing systems for highly efficient data centres.

Shares in Arm fell 6pc on the news that Mr Haas had been sounded out, which was first reported by the Financial Times.

Nvidia’s board subsequently confirmed that it had not “formally engaged” with any candidates, but was “in the process of selecting a search firm” for the role of chief executive.

A source noted that Mr Haas had previously served under Mr Huang at Nvidia and later dealt with him during the US tech giant’s failed $40bn (£31bn) attempt to buy Arm in 2020.

Mr Haas has been thrust into the frame after Mr Huang’s resignation on Thursday.

His departure was confirmed after revelations emerged about a series of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The Nvidia chief, who founded the company more than three decades ago, admitted last Sunday that he had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, who is believed by US officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

Further reports subsequently claimed that Mr Huang, who has been married for 41 years, had engaged in affairs with two other company employees.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief, has since been appointed interim chief executive while the board seeks a permanent successor.

Donald Trump weighed in on the departure last night, suggesting that Tim Cook, the former Apple boss, should take the top job at Nvidia.

Mr Trump had previously backed Mr Huang by calling him an “honourable” man. The New York Times also reported that the US president called Mr Huang on Tuesday to urge him to fight for his job.

Nvidia’s stock has plunged 22pc since news of Mr Huang’s infidelity, taking its valuation down to around $3.8tn. It had been worth more than $5tn earlier this year.

Shares in Nvidia fell by more than 2pc on Friday, dragging down the tech-heavy Nasdaq by 0.9pc.

Mr Huang’s departure has rattled investors owing to fears of a power vacuum emerging at Nvidia, which is one of the most important companies in the AI boom.

The company’s chips are used to power cutting-edge AI tools from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI and are being installed in data centres around the world.

The market turmoil has since spread to other AI stocks, with shares in data centre developers such as CoreWeave and Nebius down by 6pc and 8pc, respectively, on Friday.

Many data centres count Nvidia as a key supplier, while the company has also invested or guaranteed hundreds of billions of dollars in funding to prop up the AI infrastructure boom.

The company does not have a clear succession plan in place, with board members still preparing to appoint headhunters to target a replacement formally.

Another mooted successor is internal candidate Ian Buck, a leading engineer within the company.

Some members of Mr Huang’s family are also senior figures at the business, including his daughter Madison, son Spencer and son-in-law Nico Caprez.

Ms Kress, until this week Nvidia’s finance chief, is understood to have increasingly clashed with Mr Huang over some of his vast spending promises for the AI boom.

Frank Lee, an analyst at HSBC, said investor confidence in the company had been “shaken as [its] leadership succession plan is unclear”.

Meanwhile, leading US senators have continued to demand an investigation into Mr Huang and Nvidia, despite his resignation.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chairman, said on Thursday: “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.”

Mr Haas and Arm were contacted for comment.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Barclays opens new Saudi office despite Houthi attacks
data.description:
Barclays is braving the conflict in the Middle East by opening a new office in Saudi Arabia despite growing Houthi attacks.

The bank said on Monday it would open a new outpost in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, marking a return to the Saudi market after more than a decade.

The re-entry is significant for the region after repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia’s financial area by the Iran-backed Houthis, including the most recent attack over the weekend, when the offices of state oil giant Saudi Aramco suffered minor damage.

Barclays’ move comes after it received a licence from Saudi Arabia’s regulator, the Capital Market Authority, to conduct investment banking in the kingdom in 2025.

The bank said the country was a “key market” for its Middle East strategy and reflected the growing “economic transformation” of the kingdom.

Majed Al Hassoun has been appointed by Barclays to lead the bank’s Saudi office. He was formerly the chief executive of State Street Saudi Arabia.

However, the move comes at a time of growing safety concerns. Strikes on the capital’s airport killed more than a dozen people and disrupted flights last month.

Riyadh’s business district has been under remote-work orders for about a month.

A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.

Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.

The threat from the Houthis has also disrupted some of the country’s most important events, including its Future Investment Initiative conference, dubbed “Davos in the desert”.

CS Venkatakrishnan, the chief executive of Barclays, had been scheduled to speak at the event, but it has been postponed until 2027.

The war has also taken a toll on Saudi Arabia’s economy. Its fiscal deficit more than doubled to $22.4bn (£16.7bn) in the third quarter this year, and its economy shrank by 3.8pc as the war disrupted crude oil exports.

Mr Venkatakrishnan said: “The opening of our Riyadh office marks an important step in our growth in Saudi Arabia and across the Middle East. It strengthens our ability to support clients in the Kingdom, connecting them to the full strength of Barclays’ global business.”

data.title: Burnham to halt wind and solar subsidies in net zero climbdown
data.description:
Andy Burnham has ordered a halt to new wind and solar power subsidies in a net zero climbdown aimed at cutting household energy bills.

The Government revealed on Tuesday that next year’s auction of contracts for difference (CfDs) – a form of state support for renewable energy projects – will be paused to ensure it benefits consumers.

This year’s auction, known as auction round eight, is expected to continue as normal in the coming weeks. It is expected to award subsidies that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds a year, paid for by households and businesses.

But Michael Shanks, the energy minister, told the House of Lords environment committee that next year’s auction was being put on hold so that the CfD programme could be reformed.

It follows concerns that the development of renewable power capacity is moving faster than work to upgrade the electricity grid.

This has resulted in network bottlenecks and vast amounts of power going to waste. It has also led to wind farms being paid hundreds of millions of pounds to switch off, a practice known as “curtailment”.

Mr Shanks told peers that the Government was drawing up a new plan to prevent too much future capacity being built in Scotland, which is behind the biggest bottlenecks. He said the way subsidies are awarded will also change.

CfDs are the UK’s flagship mechanism for supporting renewable energy projects and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.

They ensure generators are always paid a fixed strike price for the electricity they produce, regardless of market prices.

Developers win CfDs by putting forward projects and bidding for fixed prices in auctions, helping to ensure the strike prices are competitive.

Last year’s estimated CfD budget was £1.7bn, covering wind farms, solar farms and other clean technologies.

“The CfD process has been incredibly useful to give investors certainty to build new projects,” Mr Shanks said. But he added that “we do now want to pause” before the next auction round to “look at whether we need some more significant changes to the contracts for difference scheme to make sure they work for the consumers of the country”.

John Healey, the Chancellor, declared in last week’s Budget that Labour’s priority was “first and foremost cheaper energy”.

Whitehall sources told The Telegraph that his remarks signalled a demotion of the 2030 clean power targets championed by Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, when he ran the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

Dan Tomlinson, a Treasury minister, said after the Budget that Mr Burnham would pursue “a new energy pathway” to “bring energy costs down to help British business to compete and British households to cope”.

Pointing to the rising cost of wasted wind power, Mr Tomlinson said: “With growing constraint and distribution costs, it’s right that the system costs of all new power are considered.”

He added that the UK would “only procure clean power” through auction round eight “if we are confident it will lower bills” and “we will reform the contract for difference [for the next auction] to support building the lowest cost system, fixing market distortions and siting assets in the right place”.

Ministers have also imposed a moratorium on new levies and policy costs being added to bills.

The Government insists that it stands by the 2030 clean power targets, which aim to ensure that 95pc of electricity generated by the end of the decade comes from “clean” sources such as renewables, nuclear or batteries.

However, ministers have sought to downplay the commitment.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, told MPs last month that it would be “pretty hard” to deliver clean power while keeping bills down, having previously said that affordability was her top concern.

She also told a conference that while her department would “play its part” to try and reach Mr Miliband’s target, “the public doesn’t measure the success of our energy system in gigawatts – they measure it in bills”.

James Alexander, chief executive of the UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association, which represents pension funds and other big financial backers, said: “Investors will be deeply concerned by comments from the energy minister today that cast doubt on next year’s renewable energy auction.”

He added: “The Contracts for Difference model has been a crucial driver of investment in clean power, helping to secure record offshore wind capacity this year and build a world-leading renewables sector.

“But telling markets the Government intends to review this process risks sending a worrying signal about the strength of the UK’s commitment to the energy transition.

“We now need to see urgent clarity on the future of this process, or the Government could put billions of pounds of capital at risk.”

The Government has been approached for comment.

data.title: Veterans forced to take 5am rail replacement bus to Remembrance Sunday
data.description:
Veterans have been offered a rail replacement bus at nearly 5am to reach Remembrance Sunday events in London.

Major Christopher McLean, 67, from Wiltshire, said the arrangements were “not good enough” and would prevent fellow veterans attending memorials.

In an email seen by The Telegraph, the Royal British Legion warned Cenotaph Parade ticket-holders that rail engineering works would bring disruption on Nov 8.

The charity advised veterans that South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex were offering limited one-way bus travel from Winchester and Salisbury railway stations that were departing at 4.45am to arrive at London Waterloo at 8am.

Scheduled replacement bus services are also operating, requiring changes between rail and bus services to arrive in London on time.

Major McLean, who lives outside Salisbury, told The Telegraph that the disruption meant he would have to get up at 3.45am, which was not ideal at his age.

“No one seems to have thought this through,” he told The Telegraph, adding: “If I had planned like that in my Army logistics career, I would have been sacked.”

Veterans forced to ‘make other arrangements’

Major McLean said that veterans would be prevented attending events in the capital because of the disruption.

He said: “Lots of us are in our 70s. What about the implications for people who are infirm? It’s not good enough. Most of the guys I know are going to have to make other arrangements.

“Luckily, I can go up the night before and stay with relatives in Surrey. If I hadn’t had family there, I would have pulled out.

“Others are looking at paying for two nights in a London hotel, which is expensive. The Royal British Legion does a great job getting this all together, but the wider logistics haven’t been considered properly.”

Veterans would have been able to leave closer to 7am if the trains were running. This would still have allowed them enough time to arrive in Whitehall, pass through police security procedures and form up on the Cenotaph for 10.30am.

Major McLean said the rail disruption was the latest woe to be bestowed on veterans.

He said: “Prosecutions of veterans, underfunding of defence – it’s one thing after another, which is really upsetting this community. This is the latest mark of disrespect.”

Veteran’s fiercely oppose Labour’s Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently in the House of Lords, arguing that it does not adequately protect former service members.

Col Richard Kemp, a retired British Army officer who served from 1977 to 2006, criticised the lack of foresight by the railway operators.

“This is probably the most important day of the year when people can come together and pay respects to the war dead,” he said, adding: “It should be given priority above other events.

“Veterans should be treated with the utmost respect, including by the railway companies. This clearly isn’t good enough.”

Last month, the Government announced that it was extending free railway travel on Remembrance weekend, which currently covers serving military staff, veterans and one next of kin of a service-person who died while serving.

However, networks across the country will be disrupted by engineering work on Nov 7 and 8.

South Western Railway, the first operator to be renationalised by Labour in May 2025, apologised to veterans whose journeys would be affected.

A spokesman said: “South Western Railway is proud of its commitment to the Armed Forces community and this year received the Ministry of Defence Gold Award.

“Unfortunately, long-planned and essential engineering works this weekend mean veterans will need to use a combination of train and rail replacement services to travel to London Waterloo.

“We investigated whether the engineering works could be rescheduled, but this would have meant deferring essential track maintenance to maintain the long-term safety and reliability of the railway.”

A spokesman for the Royal British Legion said: “We’ve worked with the rail authorities to contact veterans affected by planned engineering works so they know a rail replacement service has been arranged.”

data.title: Twelve flights diverted across Europe after bomb threats
data.description:
Twelve flights have been diverted across Europe following a series of bomb threats.

Thursday’s disruption comes days after similar incidents in which eight planes, including three from the UK, were grounded over what Britain dismissed as a “malicious hoax”.

Three of Thursday’s incidents involved flights bound for Italy.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Normandy following a bomb alert, the French prime minister’s office said.

The office of Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said all 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and that military bomb defusal teams were examining the plane.

A Finnair flight bound for Helsinki landed in Rome after a threat was reported on board, while a Wizz Air service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

A Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem airport in Belgium after the crew received a “suspicious report concerning a flight to Brussels airport”.

Three more aircraft were forced to land at airports in Bulgaria following bomb threats. 

Two of the planes – travelling from Copenhagen and Madrid respectively – landed in Sofia, the broadcaster bTV, citing the interior minister, reported.

A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv, according to reports. Four planes flying to Prague had been the subject of bomb threats and were preparing to land, according to Czech police. 

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest was also targeted, Romanian intelligence services said.

On Thursday morning, Spanish authorities said three flights at Madrid were affected by hoax threats.

None of the threats reported this week have been found to be genuine, despite triggering dozens of unplanned landings as well and escorts by fighter jets.

The EU’s transport commissioner said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether Thursday’s spate of bomb threats were linked.

Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a message posted on LinkedIn that he had asked EU security authorities “to cooperate closely with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement authorities” over the bomb threats.

On Tuesday, at least seven planes were subjected to threats. A flight to Sofia was similarly affected on Monday.

An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome. An Israel-bound cruise ship was also searched for bombs in Greece.

A British Government spokesman told The Telegraph that the threats against the UK flights had been a “malicious hoax”, though it was not clear how they had been orchestrated.

Speculation quickly centred on Moscow, with a former MI6 intelligence officer telling The Telegraph that it was his first thought when he learned of the bomb threats, which he said fitted “a pattern of behaviour” by the Kremlin.

The flight disruption follows a week of chaos, with dozens of supermarket fridges across Europe hacked on Monday. The attacks caused large amounts of food to spoil after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and turned up their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Hackers also targeted France’s national blood bank, raising the temperature of its cold storage rooms to boiling point.

Facilities at Coolworld were heated to 110C overnight on Sunday after hackers gained access to the temperature settings remotely, Le Canard enchaîné reported. The rooms are normally kept at -30C to preserve donor blood samples.

An on-duty technician detected the unusual rise in temperatures. France’s health ministry said there had been no consequences for patients and no plasma had been destroyed.

The Kremlin said European media accusations of Russian involvement in ‌cyber attacks on supermarkets were not backed up by any evidence.

Dmitry ⁠Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on Thursday: “These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely ‌no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have ⁠such ⁠baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything.”

However, pro-Russian hackers have claimed responsibility for the cyber attacks on fridges.

The pro-Russian hacking collective NoName057(16) claimed to have worked with Z-Pentest, another pro-Russian hacker group, to launch the attack.

A video claiming responsibility for the attack was posted on Telegram, according to the Danish media outlet DR.

In the video, titled Operation Chronicle: Danfoss, the hackers claimed to have “dealt a crushing blow to Danfoss and Dixell XWEB equipment”.

Danfoss and Dixell XWEB were the refrigeration companies targeted in the cyber attack.

“We didn’t even need malware for that. We just exploited the systems’ built-in features,” the hackers said.

data.title: Burnham to make new North Sea drilling illegal
data.description:
Andy Burnham is poised to ban drilling for new oil and gas in the UK to end exploration in the North Sea.

The Prime Minister has backed an energy bill that would put into law a permanent prohibition on new drilling, a move to make it harder for ministers to reverse the ban in future.

Energy exploration in the UK is subject to the temporary moratorium originally imposed by Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, but this could be lifted by a future energy secretary.

Mr Burnham is now supporting new laws being introduced by Mr Miliband’s successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, that would make it harder to reopen the North Sea.

Repealing the proposed new law would need a parliamentary majority.

The Government said the energy independence bill would deliver on its “pragmatic approach to the North Sea, by ending new licences to explore new oil and gas fields while supporting continued production from existing licensed areas”.

If approved by Parliament, the new laws would allow oil companies to keep operating existing licensed oil and gas fields until they are depleted.

But they would be able to drill new wells only if they could be connected to existing infrastructure by subsea pipelines known as tiebacks.

The move follows the approval last month of the Jackdaw gas field, which operates under an existing licence and uses a tieback to pump gas into established pipelines.

Labour is yet to make a decision on the giant Rosebank oil field, west of Shetland, which also has an existing licence.

Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have pledged to restart North Sea exploration and drilling were they to win power.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, criticised Mr Burnham’s plans warning: “Labour’s so-called energy independence bill will only make Britain more dependent on oil and gas imports. Labour might as well hang a ‘closed for business’ sign over our North Sea.”

The legislation honours Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge, which stated: “We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis. In addition, we will not grant new coal licences and will ban fracking for good.”

Some energy insiders and investors disagree, including Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos group.

David Bucknall, the head of subsidiary Ineos Energy, which has a raft of North Sea assets, said: “The Government’s legislation to ban new drilling in the North Sea would actively decrease energy security in the UK.

“Leaving existing resources in the ground at home while we import the same resources from abroad makes our energy autonomy a victim of global instability.”

Analyst Ashley Kelty, from Panmure Liberum, said: “This bill just highlights the lunacy of net zero dogma.

“It’s risible that they try to say that it’s pragmatic to stop the UK producing more oil and gas. It’s clearly a reaction to poor polling against the Greens. I see this as more vibe driven policy making as opposed to ‘pragmatic’ policy making.”

Dan Slater, from Zeus Capital, said: “While banning new exploration licences via legislation makes resumption a more circuitous process, the logic for new licences is inescapable, and parliament is sovereign and fully has the power to reverse the new ban.”

David Whitehouse, the chief executive of Offshore Energies UK, a trade body for Britain’s oil and gas producers, said the planned bill would simply make the UK more dependent on imported oil and gas.

“This will leave households and businesses exposed in an increasingly volatile world. We should be making the most of the energy we produce here at home rather than relying on imports.”

data.title: Summer heatwaves caused blackouts, admits National Grid
data.description:
Soaring temperatures triggered a rise in energy blackouts during the summer, the National Grid admitted.

The utility giant told investors on Thursday that its network suffered “additional localised outages” in June, July and August, as the heat disrupted the infrastructure distributing power to homes and businesses.

National Grid revealed details of the blackouts in its latest half-year results on Thursday.

“In UK Electricity Distribution, network stability was maintained, but additional localised outages were experienced because of the significant increase in extreme heat during the UK summer period,” the company said.

The admission comes after one of the grid’s toughest summers.

Power networks typically come under heightened pressure during cold, still winter evenings, but multiple heatwaves created a supply pinch this year.

In early August, National Grid Electricity Distribution issued formal alerts and text messages directly to customers across the Midlands and the South, warning that power cuts were increasingly probable.

National Grid’s distribution business is responsible for powering 19 million homes across the East and West Midlands, South Wales and South West England, operating 137,000 miles of lines and cables.

Much of its infrastructure is decades old, leaving it more vulnerable to extreme weather.

Sustained heat prevents underground cables and transformers from cooling overnight, significantly increasing the risk of trips and faults.

Further disruption

The UK’s 14 distribution networks carry power from the high-voltage transmission system to homes and businesses. In England and Wales, the transmission system is owned by National Grid but managed day to day by the National Energy System Operator (Neso).

In June and July, Neso was forced to issue a series of “margin warnings” seeking extra supplies to meet rising demand for air conditioning and other cooling products.

Neso said that no blackouts occurred in July and August, but reports since have highlighted how precarious the situation was.

Whistleblowers from within Neso’s control room alleged that the grid operator underplayed how fragile margins were during the June heatwave, prompting an independent inquiry that raised issues over transparency.

National Grid’s latest admission will heighten concern that the UK is becoming increasingly vulnerable to weather-related disruption.

This is partially because of climate change, but experts also point to a growing reliance on intermittent renewables and the Grid’s ageing infrastructure.

This came to the fore last year when a major fire broke out at National Grid Electricity Transmission’s North Hyde substation in Hayes, west London.

The blaze erupted when an insulating component failed on one of the main transformers, igniting approximately 25,000 litres of cooling oil.

Nearby residents were evacuated as emergency crews tackled the fire, which cut power to 67,000 domestic and commercial customers.

Crucially, the outage severed the primary supply to Heathrow and three major data centres, forcing the airport to shut down for a day.

A subsequent investigation led by Neso, Ofgem and the London Fire Brigade found that the fire was caused by water entering the transformer – a problem detected seven years previously but left unresolved by National Grid.

National Grid said it had “taken further action” to strengthen its operations since the fire, such as carrying out additional risk assessments and retesting the resilience of substations.

A spokesman for the company told The Telegraph: “Our borrowing programme helps reduce our cost of capital and with it, the cost of developing critical infrastructure in the UK. 

“This translates into savings for bill payers. Our business is financially strong. Our UK investment programme is on track, and we have substantially locked in our supply chain, giving us good visibility on costs, delivery and future cash flows. 

“The ratings agencies and financial markets monitor our ability to service our debt, which is reflected in our investment-grade credit ratings.”

data.title: M&S’s luxury cookie craze helps it buck the cost of living crisis
data.description:
It has to be one of the most dramatic rehabilitations in British retail history. Just 18 months ago the reputation of Marks & Spencer lay in tatters, its shelves denuded of food following a catastrophic cyber-hack that cost it more than £300m.

But over the past week M&S has sealed its status as the champion of high-end food and drink in a turnaround that has all but banished memories of last year’s traumatic 15-week disruption.

Where once the retailer was seen as irredeemably fuddy-duddy and middle-aged, the company’s M&S Food brand has now been enthusiastically adopted by young Gen Z and Millennial shoppers.

Such is the viral reputation of some M&S product launches that they have triggered chaotic scenes when the goodies arrive in stores.

Last week shoppers scrambled to get their hands on new batches of Chocolate & Cornflake Cookies when they turned up at the bakery counter of an M&S branch in Islington, north London.

Recent food innovations which have captivated young shoppers also include luxurious creation ranging from olive oil and lobster crisps, priced at £3.90 a pack, and white and milk chocolate-enrobed frozen strawberries costing £5.50 a tub.

In part this is down to a relentless focus on new products under M&S Food boss Alex Freudmann that has left rivals scrambling in the dust.

The company’s product-development team of around 100 people launched more than 850 new food lines in the first half of the year alone.

Fuelling the excitement about the brand has been the remarkable online phenomenon that is Kathryn Turner, M&S’s food director of product development.

She is now one of Britain’s most followed food influencer social media stars with 3.3 million TikTok likes and a 230,000-strong Instagram following that includes Nigella Lawson and Stormzy.

For Stuart Machin, Marks’ chief executive, the popularity of the brand is translating into healthier profits.

Machin recently unveiled first-half results showing food sales racing ahead by 13.9pc to £5.16bn. Operating profits hit £288.6m – well clear of the £216.4m achieved in 2024, the year before the hack.

The company set out to investors on Tuesday its hugely ambitious target of doubling food sales “over time”, having grown them by more than 50pc over the past four years.

Just to seal the deal, figures from analyst Worldpanel by Numerator suggest that demand for its food sales is still accelerating, surging by 14.6pc in the 12 weeks to Nov 1.

Internal Worldpanel figures seen by The Telegraph point to an even more significant landmark.

They show that M&S has grown its market share by volume to 3.66pc in the four weeks to Nov 1, carving out clear blue water in the race with its great rival for middle-class shopper affections, Waitrose, which had a market share of 3.14pc.

In a sluggish market where many of its competitors are struggling to eke out any positive like-for-like growth at all, the M&S performance is all the more remarkable.

Crucially, this has given M&S the financial headroom to promise shareholders a doubling of the dividend this year.

As Dan Coatsworth, at brokers AJ Bell, put it: “Marks & Spencer shareholders should be jumping for joy.” And if the stock market reaction is anything to go on – they are.

Shares in the FTSE 100 retailer gained more than 4pc on Tuesday, to close at 455.4p, the highest level in more than 11 years.

The turnaround has left analysts purring with admiration. “That is simply super impressive growth”, said retail watcher Richard Lim.

The roots of the renaissance can be traced back to Machin’s appointment as M&S managing director of food in 2018. It was just a year after former boss Archie Norman had arrived as chairman.

The pair set out to recover from what they saw as a low point in M&S’s illustrious history as a food retailer.

As Norman told The Telegraph: “When we started, the business was flatlining, had lost its edge on product, was too expensive, and 30pc sold on promotion. The new stores were small and grew to a low level of sales focussed just on convenience.

“Supply chain was outsourced to another company with whom M&S was constantly in dispute. And it had no presence online. So the early stage was very much about sorting out the basics.”

The two executives scoured the world for the grocers that inspired them, learning lessons from retailers including Trader Joe’s in America, Mercadona in Spain, Esselunga in Milan and Erewhon in California.

Another transformative decision was the development of the new-format food-only stores. The first opened in Clapham, south London, in 2019 and was an instant success, proving that “we could trade out of bigger space and be more ambitious,” according to Norman.

Now huge food-only M&S stores in affluent neighbourhoods such as Chiswick and Richmond in west London are taking the battle to Waitrose in its own affluent heartlands.

Another key change was junking M&S’s former reluctance to stock grocery staples such as flour, sugar, washing-up liquid and pet food.

You might be able to buy some nice luxuries at M&S, but you would need to go to Tesco or Asda to complete your weekly shop.

Under Machin’s leadership, M&S has deliberately become a “shopping list” grocer, where a family can stock up for the whole week in a single visit.

M&S’s unlikely success has coincided with a particularly gloomy period in Britain’s recent history when the cost of living crisis has shut off avenues of pleasure for families struggling just to pay the gas bill.

However, at a time when the cost of eating out has rocketed, an evening in with M&S has become the cheap-treat alternative to a meal in a restaurant – a phenomenon coined the “lipstick effect”.

The term was invented by Leonard Lauder, the chairman of Estée Lauder, after he noticed a surge in lipstick sales in the wake of 9/11. In anxious times consumers turn to affordable treats to give themselves a much needed morale boost.

It is a field of retailing that M&S has come to dominate. Not the everyday grocery staples, but the foodie dopamine hits that makes life feel just a little bit less troubling.

As Lim put it: “There are lots of households in the UK that on an regular ad hoc basis used to say, ‘Let’s go out to Pizza Express or Zizzi’s, it’s only going to cost us £30 or £40.’ Now, for a family of four, it is the best part of £100 and that is just not sustainable.

“So now people say, ‘Let’s have a night in at home and get something nice in to eat.’ That food-treats market is a market that M&S owns.”

data.title: BT loses £200m as households ditch landlines
data.description:
BT is facing a £200m hit as customers give up their landlines during a digital switchover.

The telecoms giant said it expected revenues to be between £150m and £200m lower this year as some customers ditch their landlines rather than switch to a digital alternative.

BT said the decline was temporary and would be offset by higher take-up of its full-fibre services, while the cost of supporting customers would also fall as the switchover completes.

It came as BT shed a further 18,000 jobs over the last six months, driven by a reduction in the number of engineers needed as it reaches the end of its full-fibre broadband rollout. Total headcount stood at 90,000 at the end of September.

Landline operators are moving customers from the old copper-wire network, known as the public switched telephone network, to modern connections delivered over the internet.

BT moved 1.1 million customers over the first half of the year. However, it warned that around one million homes or businesses still rely on old copper cables, with three months to go until the switch-off at the end of January.

A BT spokesman said: “More than three million households have now made the move to a digital landline, benefitting from a safer, more reliable service ahead of the industry‑wide analogue switchover in January 2027.

“As we focus on the small minority of our customers yet to make the switch, protecting those who need extra support remains our top priority.”

The looming deadline has prompted fears that some households and businesses could be left behind.

Some customers who fail to switch by the end of January will be placed on a temporary emergency phone service, but others risk being cut off altogether.

The transition was originally scheduled to be completed by the end of 2025, but the deadline was pushed back amid fears that elderly customers were being put at risk.

Two Virgin Media O2 customers died after their telecare devices stopped working following the switchover, while concerns have also been raised that digital landlines are more vulnerable to outages in the event of storms or cyber-attacks.

Providers have begun giving customers battery packs that can keep their landlines running during a power failure.

BT is also in discussions with the Government and Ofcom about a wider switch-off of its copper network that would also include broadband connections.

As a result of the additional costs, BT’s service revenue is expected to stand between £15.1bn and £15.4bn for the full year, compared with £15.4bn last year.

However, BT reported its first revenue increase in two and a half years, and pre-tax profit also rose in the six-month period, suggesting its turnaround plans are starting to pay off.

Higher handset sales drove the performance, while BT cut £312m in costs in the first half of the year, putting it halfway to its £3.5bn target.

BT’s Openreach division shed a further 366,000 broadband customers in the first half of the year amid fierce competition from start-up rivals, though this marked an improvement on last year’s losses.

BT also passed 10 million connections on its full-fibre network and is on track to hit its target of reaching 25 million homes in March.

Shares rose 5pc after bosses increased the interim dividend to 2.5p per share.

It comes at a turbulent time for Britain’s fiercely competitive broadband market as rivals including Virgin Media O2 and CityFibre grapple with the soaring costs of their debt-fuelled network rollouts.

BT last month struck a £400m deal to rescue stricken broadband provider TalkTalk, with ministers stepping in to override competition concerns.

The deal is undergoing a regulatory review, and Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, is expected to issue a final decision shortly.

data.title: Mercedes suspends all future investment in Germany
data.description:
Mercedes-Benz has suspended all future investment in Germany, warning it may need to shut plants and relocate jobs.

The carmaker has suffered from shrinking sales and profits in recent years, triggering a wave of cost-cutting which has culminated in a decision to stop investing in its domestic plants entirely.

Michael Schiebe, the production director, told employees: “The executive board has jointly decided to halt all further investments in German sites.”

Britta Seeger, the company’s workforce chief, said bosses would now “examine specifically and in detail which locations we can still afford in Germany”.

It comes amid a showdown between management and unions over the company’s cost-cutting plans.

The car giant, which is based in Stuttgart, has for months been pushing a plan under which its staff would work longer hours for the same pay.

The trade union, IG Metall, has pushed back, and Ms Seeger said “no solution is currently in sight”.

“If we don’t reach an agreement, we will take very tough steps,” she said.

Mercedes, like its fellow German giants Volkswagen (VW) and BMW, is battling a slump in sales in China, which was once a major source of growth.

Chinese sales of Mercedes models dropped 8pc in the third quarter compared to a year earlier. Drivers in China have either closed their wallets or are buying cheaper, domestically made cars.

Meanwhile, German carmakers are struggling to compete against an influx of cheaper Chinese cars in their European home market, and have faced tariffs in the US.

Mercedes cut the forecast for its 2026 profit margin by two percentage points, to between 2pc and 3pc, last month. It said earnings would be flat.

The car giant is trying to save €800m (£668m), including through increasing the working week from 35 hours to at least 38, and potentially cutting back holiday bonuses, according to German media.

Ms Seeger said: “If we don’t increase productivity in the country and reduce costs, we can hardly invest any more here.”

The company has about 108,000 employees in Germany, comprising two thirds of its global workforce.

It has 11 plants in Germany, alongside operations in China, the US, Poland, Romania, Hungary, Spain and South Africa.

Some of its German factories are more than 100 years old, but workers fear these could be shuttered and the production moved to Eastern Europe. Mercedes’ plant in Kecskemet, Hungary, became its biggest factory this year.

Mr Schiebe said: “The cost of an hour of labour in production in Germany is sometimes up to five times higher than at locations in Eastern Europe.” 

VW doubled its planned job cuts to 100,000 in September, and is weighing up the future of four of its German plants.

BMW reported an 11pc plunge in quarterly pre-tax profit last week and said it would cut 8,000 jobs.

data.title: Virgin Atlantic to take Heathrow terminal row to competition watchdog
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s Virgin Atlantic is poised to complain to the UK competition watchdog after Heathrow decided to move the airline’s American partner to its most remote terminal.

Delta Air Lines, which has a 49pc stake in Virgin, has been told it must relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 on the southern edge of the airfield, splitting up a joint operation that the two airlines have run for a decade.

Virgin is located at Terminal 3, and Corneel Koster, its chief executive, claims that transferring between flights will take 90 minutes, putting off customers and handing an advantage to rival British Airways (BA).

Mr Koster said Virgin planned to file a complaint with the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), claiming the move threatened to undermine competition with BA, which is responsible for one in two flights at Heathrow.

Virgin and Delta share check-in and baggage facilities in Terminal 3, as well as Virgin’s luxurious Clubhouse business lounge. They also run a joint timetable, including nine daily flights to New York.

Mr Koster told The Telegraph: “We are exploring absolutely all avenues and we will go with the avenue that we believe has the highest chance of rectifying this mad idea.

“They are going to hear from us. We’re going to challenge this really hard; there’s no way we are going to accept this. We will get this reversed.”

He added: “There are a multitude of powers that could get involved. There are legal angles and there are regulatory angles, from both the CAA’s [Civil Aviation Authority] perspective and the CMA’s perspective.”

Virgin, which styles itself as Britain’s second flag carrier after BA, maintains that the only options for accommodating it and Delta together at Heathrow are Terminals 2 and 3.

However, the airport’s shake-up plan shows that Terminal 2 will be occupied by the Star Alliance, which is led by Lufthansa and United Airlines and includes no UK carriers.

Mr Koster said handing such prime real estate to a group of foreign airlines made no sense for the economy.

The row comes after Virgin called for Heathrow’s terminals to be broken up and put under the control of airlines as the price for granting the airport permission for a third runway, key to a £48bn expansion plan.

Mr Koster said a senior figure in government had suggested to him that Heathrow’s actions appeared “punitive”.

He added: “People on the outside are looking at this and coming to all sorts of conclusions about Heathrow’s motives.

“Either you don’t understand the fundamentals of aviation competition, how joint ventures work and what’s good for consumers, or you’re out to do damage.”

Heathrow said it had spent three years working on the moves to unlock space for 2.4 million more passengers a year, a plan it said would help foster competition.

It said that four other airlines would also be compelled to switch terminals, with Finnair and Japan Airlines, two BA partners, joining Delta in Terminal 4. BA and American Airlines also operate out of different terminals, albeit much closer ones.

A spokesman said the plan would “make the best use of current terminal capacity and deliver a better overall experience for passengers”, adding: “We are committed to working closely with our airline customers to deliver these changes successfully.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: Housebuilder shares slump as surging mortgage costs put off buyers
data.description:
Shares in one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders slumped after it warned that higher mortgage rates were putting off buyers.

Taylor Wimpey, which is listed on the FTSE 100, saw up to £130m wiped off its shares on Wednesday.

It now expects to sell 10,500 homes this year, down from July’s forecast of up to 10,800.

The group warned the housing market had been “challenging” during the autumn, with higher building costs combining with weaker house prices and rising interest rates for buyers.

This month, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years after warning inflation would rise close to 5pc in early 2027 as a result of the Iran war.

Jennie Daly, the chief executive of Taylor Wimpey, said: “The autumn selling season has been more subdued, as higher mortgage rates and living costs continue to reduce customer affordability.”

The housebuilder warned shareholders that it expected its adjusted operating profit to come in at the bottom of a range estimated by analysts at between £262m and £299m.

House prices rose at their slowest pace in nearly three years during October, according to a closely watched index from Nationwide.

Property values have been hit by higher mortgage rates, which have put strain on buyers.

The average five-year fixed deal with lenders stood at just under 6pc on Tuesday, up from just under 5pc on the eve of the Iran war outbreak, according to Moneyfacts.

In a further blow to the housing market, traders expect the Bank may raise interest rates again to 4.25pc in December.

Money markets suggest rates will rise to 4.75pc by July next year.

Anthony Codling, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets, said Taylor Wimpey had cut its sales forecasts as “higher mortgage rates continue to squeeze affordability”.

He added: “Pricing continues to reflect subdued market conditions.”

The company said it welcomed the Government’s Your First Home Scheme announced in the Budget last month.

The programme, expected to open for applications in February, aims to help first-time buyers purchase a new-build home with deposits as low as 2.5pc and a 20pc equity loan.

Ms Daly added: “We welcome the Government’s Your First Home Scheme to support getting people on to the property ladder.

“Our strong first-time buyer proposition and growing outlet base position us well as the scheme develops.”

Shares fell up to 5pc before recovering to be down 3pc.
